By coupling substrate tagging to ribonucleoprotein recognition, it promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteostasis and modulates stress responses, thereby influencing heat resilience and organismal longevity. In muscle, it concentrates at sarcomeric anchorage sites and the A band, supporting localized turnover and maintenance of myofibrillar components.

A blue-light–activated receptor kinase in Arabidopsis that uses a PAS/PAC sensory core to detect blue light and oxygen, then switches a C‑terminal serine/threonine kinase into an active state that autophosphorylates and modifies downstream targets. By assembling at the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane and cycling through endomembrane compartments, it transduces light cues into growth and energy programs that govern phototropism, chloroplast positioning and organization, circadian entrainment, and guard cell ion flux. FMN binding within the sensory module tunes photoreceptor activity, and transient RNA contacts likely couple signaling to localized mRNA handling.

A nucleocytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase that predominantly operates in the nucleus to phosphorylate arginine/serine-rich RNA-processing factors, thereby assembling and tuning spliceosomal machinery and nuclear body organization. By coupling ATP- and magnesium-dependent catalysis to regulated 14-3-3 binding, it coordinates RNA splicing with broader intracellular signaling, promoting cell-cycle progression and proliferation while influencing angiogenic programs and neuronal apoptosis. Its shuttling between cytoplasm and nucleus enables crosstalk between RNA maturation and cytoskeletal and membrane-associated pathways.

A single-pass cell-surface adhesion receptor that forms a heterodimer with alpha integrin subunits to mediate high-affinity attachment to extracellular matrix and cell–cell interfaces. Its large extracellular headpiece and EGF-like stalk transmit mechanical and conformational signals, while the short cytoplasmic tail assembles intracellular adaptor complexes that organize actin stress fibers and drive migration and differentiation. By coupling adhesion to integrin-mediated and TGF-β–linked signaling, it supports epithelial cohesion and endodermal development within the integrin complex at the plasma membrane.

A nucleocytoplasmic recombination scaffold that uses an ATP-responsive RecA-like core to assemble and regulate DNA repair complexes. It promotes homologous recombination and is specifically required for resolving interstrand cross-links, thereby safeguarding genome integrity. By concentrating at telomeric chromatin and coordinating damage-responsive assemblies, it supports telomere maintenance and couples repair to cell-cycle control through multivalent protein interactions.

An ATP-dependent acyl-CoA–forming ligase that activates long-chain and very long-chain fatty acids to their CoA thioesters, thereby supplying acyl-CoA pools for β-oxidation and membrane lipid synthesis. Operating at endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria-associated ER membranes, and associating with lipid droplets and other membrane systems, it channels fatty acids toward energy production and lipid assembly. By governing acyl-CoA availability, it modulates prostaglandin output and broader lipid transport pathways that collectively support cell growth and membrane biogenesis.

A Golgi-resident, single-pass type II membrane glycosyltransferase that transfers galactose from UDP-galactose to terminal acceptors, thereby building β1,4-galactose linkages on keratan sulfate and on precursors of complex glycolipids. By installing these modifications in the Golgi lumen, it drives keratan sulfate assembly and supports downstream sphingolipid and amine-sugar–derived polymer pathways. Its luminal catalytic core and cytosolic anchor cooperate to position donor and acceptor sugars, enabling efficient UDP-galactose–dependent transfer and coordinating with neighboring glycosylation machinery.

A lysosome-targeted cysteine endopeptidase that is synthesized with an autoinhibitory prodomain and activated in acidic endosomal and lysosomal compartments to drive bulk proteolysis and selective substrate processing. By executing endopeptidase reactions within endosomes and lysosomes and, when released or secreted, outside the cell, it contributes to protein catabolism, extracellular matrix and basement membrane remodeling, and modulation of inflammatory and ion-channel pathways. Its soluble luminal state and transient membrane association position it at the heart of endolysosomal degradation and matrix turnover.

A nucleocytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase that belongs to the SR protein kinase lineage and uses ATP-dependent catalysis to phosphorylate arginine/serine-rich regions of RNA-binding proteins. By processively modifying SR-related substrates, it remodels ribonucleoprotein assemblies and regulates RNA processing and transport between cytoplasm and nucleus. This phosphorylation program integrates with broader signaling pathways that shape skeletal muscle development and other phosphorylation-dependent processes.

A small single-pass membrane subunit of the mitochondrial cytochrome b-c1 complex that stabilizes and helps assemble complex III. By reinforcing the architecture of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase machinery, it supports electron transfer from ubiquinol to cytochrome c and the proton-coupled Q cycle within the inner mitochondrial membrane. Its assembly role secures a mature, functional complex that sustains respiratory electron flow and oxidative phosphorylation.

A nuclear chromatin-associated E3 ubiquitin ligase that orchestrates postreplication and interstrand cross-link repair. Its N-terminal ligase core catalyzes ubiquitin transfer, a central ubiquitin-recognition module targets the enzyme to damaged replication sites, and a C-terminal chromatin/DNA-tethering module anchors the complex on chromatin. By assembling and stabilizing repair assemblies at stalled forks, it promotes lesion bypass and fork recovery through tightly coupled ubiquitin signaling and nucleic-acid/chromatin engagement.

A large nuclear scaffold that organizes repressive chromatin assemblies in fission yeast. It uses a C-terminal zinc-finger module to anchor at specific chromatin neighborhoods and employs extensive upstream regions to recruit remodeling and deacetylation machinery. By concentrating these assemblies, it promotes epigenetic silencing at the mating-type locus and other heterochromatic territories, coordinating with NuRD-associated pathways to stabilize transcriptionally repressed chromatin across pericentric, subtelomeric, and rDNA regions.

A mitochondrial monooxygenase that advances coenzyme Q assembly by hydroxylating a hydrophobic benzoquinone intermediate on the matrix-facing side of the organelle. Its ferritin-like catalytic core binds di-iron and activates molecular oxygen to install a specific hydroxyl group, thereby driving the pathway toward mature ubiquinone needed for mitochondrial respiration. The enzyme likely operates as a soluble catalyst that associates with membrane-proximal ubiquinone-synthesis assemblies to channel intermediates efficiently.

A cytoplasmic RNA-binding scaffold that uses three tandem double-stranded RNA-binding modules to recognize structured RNAs and assemble small-RNA effector pathways. By homodimerizing and organizing processing and effector complexes, it promotes maturation of pre-miRNA and siRNA intermediates and activates partner enzymes during RISC loading. Its dsRNA-driven assemblies integrate antiviral signaling with post-transcriptional repression, stabilizing associated proteins and dampening cell proliferation. The complex operates primarily in the cytosol with transient residence in the nucleoplasm and at membrane-proximal RNA assemblies.

A cytoplasmic, membrane-proximal regulator that uses an N-terminal catalytic module to accelerate GTP hydrolysis on ARF-class small GTPases while tandem phosphoinositide-binding domains target the enzyme to specific membrane sites. By coupling catalytic inactivation of ARF signaling with spatial control through dual PH modules, it tunes endocytic and recycling pathways that shape receptor signaling. A soluble cytosolic pool and peripheral membrane association enable dynamic shuttling between membrane and cytoplasm, with occasional nuclear transit likely coordinating trafficking-derived signals with gene regulatory programs.

A cell-surface receptor-like protein in Arabidopsis that presents a large extracellular leucine-rich repeat scaffold to bind peptide signals and maintain the root stem cell niche. It operates at the plasma membrane after secretory-pathway maturation, where it perceives root meristem cues and, lacking intrinsic catalytic activity, signals by assembling membrane co-receptors and adaptor kinases. This mechanism modulates meristem growth and identity and promotes proper phloem differentiation and broader cell differentiation programs.

A membrane-associated small GTPase switch in Arabidopsis that cycles between GTP- and GDP-bound states to assemble kinase- and phosphatase-rich signaling hubs. By organizing effectors at the cell surface, it coordinates assembly and remodeling of the plant cell wall and tunes cellulose and beta-glucan synthesis. The same assemblies attenuate abscisic acid–activated pathways, particularly in guard cells and stress-responsive tissues. Its activity is centered at the plasma membrane with functional coupling to wall biogenesis and transient nuclear signaling pools.

A soluble flavoenzyme in Rhizobium meliloti that initiates thiamine degradation by coupling a TIM-barrel catalytic core to a dinucleotide-binding module. It binds a flavin cofactor and uses pyridine nucleotide–driven electron transfer to reduce a pyridoxal-derived imine intermediate, thereby launching the first committed step of thiamine catabolism. The enzyme likely operates in a cytosolic catalytic assembly that coordinates sequential reactions and balances redox equivalents during amino-acid–derived metabolite breakdown.

An atypical seven-transmembrane receptor in rat that binds inflammatory chemokines with high affinity and rapidly internalizes them through endocytic pathways. By capturing and trafficking CCL2 and CCL8 from the cell surface into endosomal and lysosomal compartments, it scavenges chemokines, stabilizes extracellular gradients, and thereby enhances chemotaxis. Although it adopts a rhodopsin-like fold, it functions primarily as a chemokine interceptor and gradient shaper rather than a classical G-protein signal transducer, cycling between the plasma membrane and intracellular compartments with cytoplasmic and nucleus-proximal signaling assemblies.

A multi-pass plasma membrane receptor in fission yeast that senses extracellular glucose through an N-terminal sugar-binding module and transduces the signal via a transmembrane core to activate heterotrimeric G protein–coupled pathways. By assembling cytosolic signaling complexes that stimulate adenylate cyclase and elevate cAMP, it drives glucose-responsive signaling while suppressing mating and conjugation programs under nutrient-replete conditions.

A large cytoplasmic actin-regulatory scaffold that concentrates at filamentous actin structures and binds tropomyosin to organize and stabilize actin assemblies. By using a gelsolin-like core and a C-terminal headpiece to anchor onto actin/tropomyosin substrates, it assembles multivalent complexes that tune filament architecture and thereby modulate contractile machinery. This positioning and scaffolding role supports the regulation of muscle contraction by coordinating actomyosin systems within the actin cytoskeleton.

A soluble catalytic subunit of the human molybdopterin synthase complex that drives assembly of the molybdenum cofactor. It operates as a cytosolic enzyme that binds partner proteins to form an active hetero-assembly, channeling sulfur-transfer chemistry that matures the pterin scaffold en route to the cofactor. Its activity supports the maturation and delivery of the cofactor to downstream molybdoenzymes. The enzyme resides primarily in the cytosol and cytoplasm, associates with the molybdopterin synthase complex, and can transiently concentrate at nuclear speckles where macromolecular assemblies coordinate metabolic and RNA-processing functions.

A GPI-anchored surface coat protein in Trypanosoma that assembles into a dense, renewing layer on the parasite’s membrane to mediate antigenic variation. Its N-terminal scaffold drives multivalent binding and lattice formation that shields invariant surface molecules, while its C-terminal region directs GPI addition and secretory trafficking to the cell surface. By combining high-density surface display with rapid turnover and endocytic clearance, it enables immune evasion through continual replacement of the exposed antigenic coat.

A cytosolic copper/zinc-dependent superoxide dismutase that forms a soluble β-barrel enzyme complex to convert superoxide into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, thereby protecting cells from oxidative damage. Its soluble architecture positions it as a primary buffer for intracellular superoxide, shaping downstream responses to xenobiotics and inorganic stimuli and modulating hydrogen peroxide signaling. Operating predominantly in the cytoplasm and functionally coupled to peroxisome-proximal redox pathways, it likely receives copper via dedicated chaperones and collaborates with other antioxidant systems to maintain redox balance.

A soluble, homodimeric antioxidant enzyme in cattle that uses tightly bound copper and zinc to catalyze the rapid conversion of superoxide into hydrogen peroxide and oxygen. Its β-barrel architecture enforces metal-dependent catalysis and dimerization, enabling efficient detoxification of reactive oxygen species and shaping downstream redox signaling. Enriched in neuronal cell bodies and dendritic cytoplasm, it assembles into cytosolic complexes that localize ROS handling and indirectly enhance broader antioxidant capacity.

A soluble antioxidant enzyme in baker’s yeast that assembles into an oxidoreductase complex to neutralize superoxide by copper- and zinc-dependent disproportionation. By removing superoxide in the cytosol and at mitochondrial interfaces, it protects proteins and membranes, stabilizes and matures client proteins, and tunes respiratory and transcriptional programs. Its metal-centered chemistry links oxidative stress defense to broader ion homeostasis and cell wall organization, with dynamic assemblies that position the enzyme in cytosolic and mitochondrial compartments and enable stress-responsive roles in the nucleus.

A soluble bacterial enzyme that binds DNA and executes the full repertoire of template-directed synthesis and end processing. It uses a C-terminal polymerase core to extend primers during strand synthesis, a central mismatch-excision module to proofread nascent DNA, and an N-terminal nuclease to remove RNA primers and 5′ flaps. By coupling these activities, it completes lagging-strand maturation and gap filling, thereby supporting chromosomal replication and repair pathways that restore DNA integrity within the cytosol.

A secreted peptide hormone that is synthesized as a prohormone and processed into multiple bioactive forms, which bind class B G protein–coupled receptors to elevate cAMP signaling and mobilize glucose stores. By stimulating gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis while suppressing glycolysis, it coordinates systemic energy balance and influences feeding-related pathways. The molecule is produced and folded in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, packaged within secretory granules, and released to the extracellular space where it engages its receptors and assembles into higher-order complexes that fine-tune signaling strength and duration.

A nuclear chromatin protein that forms a stable heterodimer with another core histone to build nucleosomes and compact DNA into chromosomal fibers. By stabilizing and remodeling nucleosome architecture, it modulates transcriptional accessibility and broader DNA-associated processes. This chromatin-scaffolding role tunes innate and mucosal immune gene programs in fruit fly, shaping antimicrobial peptide production and dampening inflammatory signaling pathways through regulated chromatin assembly and remodeling.

A nuclear chromatin-packaging histone that forms the core of nucleosomes and assembles with H2A–H2B and H2A.Z-containing particles to regulate chromatin architecture. By stabilizing and remodeling nucleosome structures, it modulates DNA accessibility and supports the formation of repressive chromatin domains. It resides on chromosomes within the nucleus, prominently visible on polytene chromosomes, and functions through multivalent binding that scaffolds nucleosome assembly and exchange to drive chromatin remodeling and heterochromatin formation.

A secreted extracellular matrix glycoprotein that assembles into basement membranes and presents multivalent binding surfaces that anchor cells and organize pericellular signaling. By building a laminin-based scaffold and engaging cell-surface receptors, it shapes morphogenesis and neural tissue patterning, particularly in the retina and glial lineages, thereby contributing to visual system development and function.

A secreted extracellular matrix subunit that assembles into a laminin heterotrimer and deposits into basement membranes, where it organizes epithelial architecture and polarity. Its N-terminal assembly module and an extended array of EGF-like repeats create a multivalent scaffold that binds numerous partners, while a C‑terminal helical tail enforces trimerization. By anchoring to integrins and other matrix components, it stabilizes epithelial–mesenchymal interfaces and supports adhesion events at tissue boundaries within collagen-rich basement membrane.

A soluble calcium-buffering protein that uses a paired EF-hand module to bind two calcium ions with high affinity, smoothing cytosolic calcium transients in excitable and epithelial cells. By rapidly sequestering and releasing calcium, it stabilizes signaling pathways important for hearing and other calcium-dependent processes. Its soluble architecture places it in the cytoplasm and, in polarized epithelia, near apical brush border regions where calcium fluxes are prominent.

A homodimeric cell-surface receptor that captures transferrin and initiates clathrin-mediated endocytosis to deliver ferric iron into endosomal pathways that maintain cellular iron balance. Its ectodomain assembles a high-avidity transferrin-binding platform, while a dimerization module enforces receptor clustering and endocytic routing. By coordinating endocytosis with intracellular signaling hubs, it promotes lymphocyte proliferation and differentiation, enhances NF-κB pathway activity, and influences mitochondrial and apoptotic programs. The receptor cycles between the external plasma membrane and endosomal system and is also incorporated into extracellular vesicles.

A secreted, vitamin K–dependent extracellular matrix protein that concentrates calcium via a γ-carboxyglutamate-rich module and anchors to the mineralizing bone matrix. By binding calcium and assembling with other matrix constituents, it helps organize hydroxyapatite deposition and coordinates osteoblast–osteoclast activities. Its production and activity integrate with glucocorticoid-responsive pathways that tune bone remodeling.

A secreted extracellular matrix protein that becomes enriched in gamma-carboxylated glutamate residues and binds calcium-rich hydroxyapatite to stabilize bone matrix. By acting as a structural adaptor within mineralized tissue, it anchors to collagenous scaffolds and helps organize the assembly and maintenance of mineralized extracellular architecture during bone formation and remodeling.

A lysosome-associated glycosidase that uses a catalytic barrel capped by a beta-sandwich to hydrolyze terminal glucosyl groups on glycoconjugates and glycosphingolipids. By editing glycans and shaping sphingolipid and ceramide flux at the lysosomal interface, it supports autophagy and lysosome organization, tunes lipidation and TOR signaling, and dampens MAP kinase and inflammatory pathways. Its soluble fold and trafficking explain cytoplasmic transit and exosome packaging, while receptor-complex contacts at endo-lysosomal membranes couple glycan remodeling to neuronal excitability and survival.

A calcium-regulated membrane-associated scaffold that binds anionic phospholipids and assembles membrane-proximal complexes to control vesicle trafficking, secretion, and cytoskeletal remodeling. Its annexin core binds calcium to trigger reversible membrane attachment, while an A1-class N-terminal segment tunes interactions that coordinate endosomal and secretory pathways. By coupling calcium sensing to membrane docking, it supports motility and secretion from a predominantly cytoplasmic, peripherally membrane-bound state.

A tegument-delivered serine/threonine kinase that enters host cells with the virion and rapidly reprograms the cellular environment to favor the viral life cycle. By using ATP-dependent phosphorylation and multivalent protein binding, it assembles repressive complexes that dampen host transcription and cell-cycle progression, while stabilizing the viral replication platform through modification of the viral DNA synthesis machinery. Its presence in both the cytoplasm and nucleus enables coordinated suppression of transcriptional outputs and remodeling of cytoskeletal and trafficking pathways that support efficient virion assembly and spread.

A soluble human enzyme that generates thymidylate for DNA synthesis by transferring and reducing one-carbon units from folate-derived donors, thereby sustaining pyrimidine nucleotide production and coupling directly to folate metabolism. It likely functions as a homodimer that binds folate cofactors and forms a transient covalent intermediate with dUMP to yield dTMP. Beyond catalysis, it moonlights as an RNA-associated factor that binds specific mRNA elements to repress translation, aligning gene expression with nucleotide and folate supply. It predominantly operates in the cytosol but also engages mitochondrial and nuclear compartments where nucleotide and DNA biogenesis are coordinated.

A cytosolic enzyme in Bacillus that uses an ATP-dependent nucleotidyltransferase mechanism to chemically modify aminoglycoside antibiotics such as kanamycin and neomycin. By assembling a catalytic core with a kanamycin-recognition module, it binds nucleotide cofactors and aminoglycoside substrates to generate an inactivated nucleotidylated product, thereby contributing to cellular resistance during antibiotic exposure.

A single-pass cell-surface adhesion receptor that forms an obligate heterodimer with alpha integrins to anchor cells to extracellular matrix and transmit bidirectional signals. Its extracellular head binds matrix ligands and organizes growth factor and chemokine cues, while a cysteine-rich stalk and short cytoplasmic tail couple to cytoskeletal and kinase assemblies. This architecture enables strong cell–matrix adhesion, platelet and vascular signaling, synaptic receptor trafficking, and broad adhesion-dependent pathways at lamellipodia, ruffles, and focal adhesions. By clustering with growth factor and receptor systems, it acts as a coreceptor that elevates and routes signaling outputs across diverse physiological processes.

A single-pass cell-surface adhesion and signaling receptor that pairs with an alpha subunit to form a high-affinity matrix-binding platform. Its extracellular head binds extracellular matrix ligands and transduces mechanical cues through a series of EGF-like stalk repeats to a membrane-proximal module and cytoplasmic tail that recruit cytoskeletal and kinase adaptors. This architecture enables coreceptor functions that coordinate adhesion with intracellular signaling, thereby controlling leukocyte rolling and adhesion, fibroblast migration and wound repair, angiogenic signaling, and lineage-specific adhesion during development and immune responses. The receptor cycles between the plasma membrane and endosomal compartments and concentrates at dynamic membrane specializations and adhesion sites.

A nucleoid-associated organizer of DNA repair in Bacillus subtilis that binds and stabilizes DNA junctions and assembles repair complexes. Its RecF-class architecture and an ATP/NTP-responsive core enable formation of mediator assemblies that capture single-stranded and branched DNA, recruit processing factors, and channel intermediates into homologous recombination and excision pathways. By scaffolding partner proteins at damaged chromosomal sites, it promotes accurate repair of double-strand breaks and broader genome maintenance.

A small, soluble calcium sensor that forms an inactive monomer which becomes an active homodimer upon calcium binding. The dimer exposes a hydrophobic interface that captures target proteins in a calcium-dependent manner, enabling assembly of membrane-proximal signaling and cytoskeletal complexes. It operates predominantly in the cytosol and perinuclear cytoplasm, concentrates at membrane ruffles and extrinsic membrane surfaces, and can be packaged into extracellular vesicles. By coupling calcium transients to target binding, it modulates pathways that coordinate actin/tropomyosin systems and broader signal transduction.

A receptor-type tyrosine phosphatase at the cell surface that uses an extracellular adhesion-like scaffold to position a cytosolic catalytic core for precise control of tyrosine phosphorylation. By assembling at membrane-proximal signaling hubs, it removes phosphate groups from signaling proteins to tune receptor pathways, especially those governing T cell signaling, thereby influencing transcriptional programs and stress responses. Its single-pass type I topology places the catalytic machinery on the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane, where it modulates pathway thresholds through reversible protein dephosphorylation and multivalent complex assembly.

A Ca2+-activated membrane adaptor in rat that cycles between the cytoplasm and organelle membranes to organize endocytic and exocytic pathways and modulate inflammatory signaling. Its annexin core binds acidic phospholipids in a Ca2+-dependent manner, enabling reversible attachment to endosomal and other intracellular membranes. Through this membrane-coupled scaffolding, it assembles trafficking and signaling modules that indirectly tune calcium movement across membranes and suppress pro-inflammatory outputs.

A soluble peroxisomal enzyme that initiates β-oxidation by oxidizing very-long-chain and branched-chain acyl-CoA substrates. It binds fatty acyl-CoA and a flavin cofactor, transfers electrons from the substrate’s C–H bonds to reduce the flavin, and uses molecular oxygen as the terminal acceptor to generate hydrogen peroxide. By producing the corresponding aldehydes that feed the peroxisomal β-oxidation spiral, it supports degradation of long- and branched-chain fatty acids within the peroxisomal matrix. The enzyme likely functions as a homodimer and operates in concert with other peroxisomal β-oxidation and oxidative-stress–handling pathways.

A soluble mitochondrial flavoprotein that initiates electron flow from NADPH to an iron–sulfur ferredoxin, thereby priming downstream monooxygenase reactions essential for steroid precursor formation. It binds NADPH and FAD through a Rossmann-like core, becomes reduced and then transfers single electrons to adrenodoxin/ferredoxin in the mitochondrial matrix. By seeding a dedicated electron relay, it sustains mitochondrial redox pathways that feed steroidogenic and other oxidative processes.

A secreted papain-like cysteine endopeptidase allergen from the European house dust mite that is produced as an autoinhibited zymogen and activated under acidic conditions to remodel extracellular substrates. By cleaving internal peptide bonds through a catalytic cysteine–histidine–asparagine triad, it efficiently degrades matrix proteins such as collagen and related components in the extracellular space, thereby driving matrix turnover and shaping allergenic peptide release.

A single-pass cell-surface receptor-type tyrosine phosphatase that presents an extracellular adhesion module and a cytosolic catalytic core to coordinate signaling at the plasma membrane. Its ectodomain organizes extracellular cue sensing and membrane anchoring, while the intracellular active site removes phosphotyrosine marks to reset signaling thresholds. By assembling kinase-rich complexes and coupling to spectrin–ankyrin cytoskeletal networks, it modulates pathways that govern signal transduction, immune receptor signaling, stress responses, and downstream gene-expression programs at the cell surface.

A cell-surface, single-pass receptor that presents an immunoglobulin-like ectodomain to capture immune-complexed targets and transduce signals across the membrane. By clustering at the external face of the plasma membrane, it initiates phosphoinositide and calcium signaling that activate cytotoxic lymphocytes and macrophages, promote natural killer cell activation and proliferation, and drive cytokine production within both innate and adaptive immune circuits. Its membrane-anchored architecture and participation in larger receptor assemblies enable robust immune effector responses and can be released in extracellular vesicles.

A secreted, vitamin K–dependent serine protease that assembles a membrane-targeted hemostatic scaffold. Its calcium- and phospholipid-binding module targets the enzyme to membrane surfaces, an adjacent EGF-like region stabilizes Ca2+-dependent assemblies and extracellular interactions, and a trypsin-like catalytic core executes endoproteolysis. Through this architecture it drives blood coagulation and extracellular proteolysis, and it modulates growth-factor and signaling pathways by forming complexes in the secretory pathway and extracellular space. It is synthesized and matured in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi lumen before functioning in the extracellular region and at membrane-proximal sites.

A membrane-proximal GTPase switch that couples activated seven-transmembrane receptors to intracellular signaling pathways. It binds and hydrolyzes GTP to control assembly and disassembly of heterotrimeric complexes at the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane and associated trafficking stations. By cycling between inactive and active states and recruiting regulatory cofactors, it modulates vesicle fusion and secretion, shapes developmental and vascular signaling programs, restrains apoptotic pathways, and interfaces with redox systems that elevate superoxide production. Its lipid-anchored topology and transient residence at membrane rafts, the Golgi, and secretory granules position it to coordinate receptor-driven control of membrane trafficking and signal transduction.

A soluble, membrane-cycling signal-transducing switch that binds and hydrolyzes GTP to control heterotrimeric G protein signaling. It assembles with beta and gamma subunits to form an inactive complex at membranes, then upon receptor-catalyzed nucleotide exchange adopts an active conformation that modulates downstream effectors. This switch coordinates pathways downstream of seven-transmembrane receptors, often dampening adenylate cyclase and tuning cAMP output. Its dynamic partitioning between cytoplasm and membranes supports roles in dopamine-responsive signaling, cell division structures, and autophagy regulation, with trafficking through secretory and endolysosomal systems and transient residence at centrosomes and the midbody.

A secreted extracellular serine endopeptidase in mouse that is produced as a zymogen and activated outside the cell to cleave target proteins in the extracellular milieu. Its chymotrypsin-like fold and catalytic triad drive peptide-bond hydrolysis, enabling modulation of extracellular pathways that can influence envenomation-like outcomes. The enzyme likely operates through transient binding to substrates and inhibitors, with zymogen activation and controlled proteolysis shaping its activity profile in the extracellular region.

A secreted serine endopeptidase in mouse that adopts the chymotrypsin-like fold and operates outside the cell to remodel extracellular protein networks in the reproductive tract. Produced as a zymogen and activated to expose a catalytic triad, it hydrolyzes peptide bonds to drive extracellular protein turnover and processing. By cleaving and modulating seminal or epididymal substrates, it likely fine-tunes sperm surface composition and motility through tightly controlled proteolysis.

A secreted serine endopeptidase that operates outside cells to remodel the pericellular environment and tune epithelial physiology. It is produced as a zymogen and activated by proteolytic processing within a classical chymotrypsin-like fold, where a histidine–aspartate–serine catalytic triad drives peptide-bond hydrolysis. By cleaving extracellular substrates and assembling with inhibitors and targets, it modulates signaling pathways that influence ion channel behavior in neighboring tissues, consistent with tissue-restricted expression in liver and kidney and a role in extracellular regulation.

A soluble bacterial transcriptional repressor that binds operator DNA via an N‑terminal winged‑helix module and forms homodimers stabilized by a C‑terminal self-cleaving regulatory core. It represses promoter-proximal sites controlling the DNA-damage inducible regulon and is switched off by RecA-stimulated autocleavage during genotoxic stress, thereby derepressing genes required for the SOS response. It operates in the cytosol and engages DNA to assemble repressive complexes that tune transcriptional outputs.

A cytoplasmic ATP-dependent recombinase that assembles into helical filaments on single-stranded DNA to drive homology search and strand exchange during recombinational repair. By coupling ATP hydrolysis to filament dynamics, it stabilizes and processes stalled replication intermediates, stimulates the DNA damage–inducible transcriptional program, and coordinates with polymerase-centered pathways to maintain chromosome integrity under genotoxic and replication stress.

A cytosolic, ATP-driven translational throttle that binds ribosomes and uses an ABC-like ATPase core to pause elongation complexes. By coupling nucleotide binding and hydrolysis to conformational changes transmitted through an extended helical module, it clamps onto paused ribosomes, halts translocation, and diverts translating assemblies into quality-control routes. This energy-dependent checkpoint thereby down-modulates bulk protein synthesis in Escherichia coli.

A multi-pass inner-membrane pump in E. coli that uses an aspartyl-phosphorylated P-type mechanism to couple ATP hydrolysis to cation translocation. Its cytosolic actuator and phosphorylation domains drive an E1/E2 cycle that energizes ion movement through a transmembrane core, tuning membrane potential and ion balance. By integrating with broader membrane systems, it contributes to cellular adjustments triggered by magnesium fluctuations at the cytoplasmic membrane.

An ATP-driven hexameric ring helicase in E. coli that assembles via its N-terminal collar and powers strand separation through a C-terminal AAA+ motor. It initiates and sustains DNA replication by unwinding duplex DNA and coordinating primer synthesis with primase and clamp loader. Operating as a soluble replisome core within the bacterial cytosol and nucleoid-associated assemblies, it stabilizes unwound templates and supports fork progression and recovery from genotoxic stress.

A soluble bacterial enzyme that uses S-adenosyl-L-methionine to methylate adenine at a defined palindromic DNA site, thereby establishing methylation patterns that tune replication initiation and direct mismatch repair. By binding specific duplex DNA and transferring a methyl group through a covalent catalytic cycle, it modulates chromosomal responses to stress, including ultraviolet challenge. Operating in the cytoplasm and transiently engaging the nucleoid, it coordinates with replication and repair assemblies to couple site-specific methylation to genome maintenance.

A soluble bacterial transcriptional regulator that binds operator DNA via an N-terminal helix-turn-helix head and uses a large allosteric core to modulate promoter occupancy. It represses transcription of its target under basal conditions and can switch to activation when intracellular cues—likely nucleotide-bound states—alter its conformation. Operating in the cytoplasm where the nucleoid resides, it fine-tunes gene expression by coupling sequence-specific DNA recognition to nucleotide-responsive allostery.

A secreted, matrix-associated mineralization factor that concentrates in bone and binds calcium-rich hydroxyapatite surfaces via a γ-carboxylated module. By anchoring to the collagen-rich extracellular matrix and coordinating calcium, it helps organize and stabilize mineral deposition sites, positioning itself to modulate crystal growth and the broader program of bone mineralization.

A secreted Kunitz-type venom inhibitor that deploys a disulfide-stabilized inhibitory loop to block trypsin-like serine proteases, thereby suppressing coagulation and fibrinolytic pathways and producing anticoagulant effects. It is released into the extracellular space but can accumulate in the cytoplasm and at the cell cortex of target tissues during cytotoxic delivery. By tightly trapping its protease targets through a canonical Kunitz inhibitory mechanism, it dampens hemostatic cascades and modulates processes in another organism.

A soluble bacterial translation factor that uses a translational GTPase core to assemble with GTP and aminoacyl‑tRNA, escort it to the ribosomal A site, and trigger accurate decoding through regulated GTP hydrolysis. Its β‑barrel scaffold stabilizes tRNA and ribosome contacts, while binding to alarmone nucleotides enables stress‑responsive tuning of elongation. Operating in the cytoplasm and cycling on and off ribosomes, it coordinates elongation efficiency with cellular nucleotide and stress signals via a guanine‑nucleotide exchange cycle.

A tandem-repeat ubiquitin-derived scaffold that assembles multivalent binding platforms to regulate selective protein turnover and signaling. By forming polymeric ubiquitin-like assemblies, it recruits conjugation and protease machineries that direct substrates toward proteasomal and endolysosomal pathways. Its soluble pools operate in the cytosol and nucleoplasm, while peripheral association with membranes supports endocytic, endosomal, ER-associated, and mitochondrial pathways. Auxiliary RNA and protease interactions couple ubiquitin-mediated degradation to ribonucleoprotein environments and vesicle-mediated communication.

A bacterial scaffold that organizes cytokinetic and envelope biogenesis machinery in Bacillus subtilis. It assembles into punctate complexes in young cells and becomes more diffuse in older cells, positioning near the nucleoid and cytoplasmic membrane interfaces. By oligomerizing through a DivIVA-like core, it recruits partner proteins to coordinate septal membrane remodeling with glycolipid production and cell division, thereby coupling chromosome-associated sites with membrane assembly pathways.

A secreted Kunitz-type venom protease inhibitor that binds and blocks trypsin-like serine proteases through a disulfide-stabilized inhibitory loop, thereby suppressing fibrinolytic pathways and stabilizing clots. By restraining thrombin/plasmin-related cascades and inhibiting elastase and trypsin in vitro, it shifts hemostatic balance toward coagulation and away from fibrin breakdown in the extracellular milieu, likely concentrating near pericellular surfaces where clot formation and lysis are coordinated.

A secreted, disulfide-rich venom protein that adopts a Kunitz inhibitory fold to bind and block serine protease active sites. It potently inhibits pancreatic trypsin and chymotrypsin in vitro and likely acts extracellularly to modulate protease-driven pathways in prey and microbes. By restraining extracellular proteolytic cascades that govern clot formation and tissue responses, it dampens hemostatic signaling and broadly modulates physiological processes in other organisms.

A secreted venom Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitor that uses a disulfide-stabilized scaffold to present a reactive loop and block the active sites of trypsin-like enzymes. It potently inhibits pancreatic trypsin and chymotrypsin in vitro and, in vivo, targets coagulation and fibrinolytic proteases such as thrombin and plasmin, thereby dampening clot formation and promoting fibrin clearance. Acting in the extracellular milieu, it modulates hemostatic pathways of the envenomed organism by forming tight inhibitory complexes that stabilize and regulate protease activity.

A secreted, disulfide-rich venom peptide that uses a Kunitz inhibitory fold to bind and reversibly block trypsin-like serine proteases. By occupying the active site with a reactive loop, it potently inhibits pancreatic and coagulation-associated enzymes such as plasmin and alpha-trypsin, thereby dampening hemostatic pathways in the extracellular milieu. This extracellular inhibition modulates protease-dependent processes in another organism and contributes to the venom’s disruption of prey hemostasis.

A secreted Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitor from Chinese bird spider venom that uses a disulfide-stabilized scaffold and a reactive inhibitory loop to bind and block trypsin-like proteases. It potently inhibits bovine pancreatic trypsin and shows moderate affinity for thrombin and chymotrypsin, thereby dampening extracellular protease cascades that drive coagulation and broader proteolytic pathways in other organisms. Acting outside cells and concentrated at cortical interfaces, it modulates hemostatic and extracellular protease networks by forming tight inhibitory complexes with target enzymes.

A secreted Kunitz-type venom inhibitor that blocks extracellular serine proteases through a disulfide-stabilized inhibitory loop, potently suppressing trypsin-like enzymes and plasmin. By dampening fibrinolysis and coagulation pathways in the extracellular space, it modulates hemostatic balance during envenomation and contributes to prey immobilization and tissue damage typical of spider venoms.

A secreted Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitor from Chinese bird spider venom that deploys a canonical inhibitory loop to block trypsin/kallikrein targets and suppress hemostatic protease cascades in the extracellular milieu. It potently inhibits human plasmin (IC50 1.5 μM), human thrombin (IC50 1.8 μM), and human plasma kallikrein (IC50 1.6 μM), and more weakly inhibits trypsin-1 and trypsin-2. By arresting these proteases outside cells, it dampens coagulation and fibrinolytic pathways in envenomed tissues, acting at the host–parasitoid interface through transient extracellular and cell-surface associations.

A soluble acyltransferase in the poison nut tree that catalyzes acyl-group transfer within specialized metabolic pathways. It operates downstream of strychnine formation to steer intermediates toward open-chain derivatives en route to phytocannabinoid scaffolds, and it also feeds into flavonoid and anthocyanin branches. The enzyme’s CAT-like catalytic core uses acyl-CoA donors to acylate reactive phenolic or amine acceptors, thereby stabilizing intermediates and directing pathway flux. Its soluble architecture and association with organellar metabolism suggest a mitochondrial-tethered role that couples acyl-donor availability and redox balance to alkaloid and flavonoid biosynthesis.

A multifunctional ribonucleoprotein that forms the structural core of the virion and organizes viral RNA into replication-competent assemblies. It uses an N-terminal assembly module and a C-terminal dimerization core to bind RNA stem-loops, homodimerize, and scaffold biomolecular condensates that concentrate viral replication machinery. By acting as an adaptor and condensate organizer in the cytoplasm and nucleus, it packages the genome for virion assembly and modulates host innate immunity, dampening interferon-beta production while tuning inflammasome assembly through transient contacts with immune complexes.

A soluble mitochondrial acyltransferase that uses an acetyltransferase-like catalytic core to transfer acyl groups from acyl-CoA donors onto alcohol and amine acceptors. By acetylating diverse hydroxyl- and amine-containing small molecules, it tunes acyl-CoA and alcohol/aldehyde pools that feed into fatty acid and specialized-metabolite routes. Operating within mitochondria, it likely shapes local acyl flux connected to volatile formation and oxylipin-related branches, functioning through a tetrahedral acyl-transfer mechanism typical of chloramphenicol acetyltransferase-like enzymes.

An essential capsid-associated scaffold that integrates into the icosahedral nucleocapsid to drive virion assembly and stability, while simultaneously dampening host innate immunity. By relying on multivalent protein–protein interactions, it organizes capsid architecture and shuttles between host cytoplasm and nucleus. This interaction-driven mechanism both stabilizes the T=16 shell and suppresses pathways that would otherwise trigger type I interferon responses, thereby coordinating virion assembly with immune evasion.

A soluble bacterial enzyme that assembles into a homooligomeric nitrilase to hydrolyze diverse nitriles into their corresponding carboxylates and ammonia. By using a cysteine-centered catalytic apparatus within a carbon–nitrogen hydrolase fold, it supports cellular nitrogen and carbon fluxes in the cytoplasm. Its broad substrate scope arises from an oligomer-stabilized tunnel that accommodates varied nitriles, thereby feeding carboxylate products into central metabolism while contributing to overall nitrogen compound turnover.

A small intracellular adaptor that organizes assemblies required for surface-associated motility in Agrobacterium. By using a compact interaction module to bind multiple partners, it scaffolds nucleoid-proximal complexes and cytoskeletal systems that collectively drive swarming. Its soluble architecture positions it within the bacterial nucleoid and cytoskeletal network, where it coordinates assembly and regulation of flagellum-dependent motility pathways through multivalent protein binding rather than catalysis.

A cytosolic aldose 1-epimerase (mutarotase) from Streptomyces that accelerates the interconversion of alpha and beta anomers of aldoses, thereby tuning entry into central carbon pathways. By rapidly equilibrating sugar anomers, it optimizes flux toward glycolytic and pentose phosphate routes and likely supports metabolic remodeling during iron-responsive states. The enzyme operates through a carbohydrate-binding groove and acid–base chemistry that transiently opens and recloses sugar rings, functioning as a soluble hub that coordinates with cytosolic sugar-metabolism enzymes.

A soluble cytoplasmic enzyme in Streptomyces that uses a sugar-phosphate–binding core to couple transamination with phosphorylation-oriented carbohydrate chemistry. By binding and orienting phosphorylated metabolites through a metal-stabilized pocket, it catalyzes nitrogen transfer reactions that feed into pyruvate/lactate balance while supporting pathways that modulate carbohydrate phosphorylation. This dual role positions the enzyme at a metabolic junction where carbon and nitrogen fluxes are integrated within the cytoplasm.

A soluble cytoplasmic enzyme in Streptomyces that contributes to biotin production through a TIM-barrel catalytic core. It likely binds carbonyl- and phosphate-bearing intermediates and executes a group-transfer step that stabilizes or channels a late-stage intermediate in the pathway, thereby ensuring efficient assembly of biotin. Although not required for the first three steps, it operates downstream where its barrel-mediated chemistry supports pathway flux and handoff to membrane-proximal assembly hubs.

An ER-embedded, single-pass type II membrane adaptor that organizes protein assemblies to tune growth factor signaling and cell-cycle entry. By anchoring multiprotein complexes at the endoplasmic reticulum, it modulates calcium handling and stress-responsive pathways that feed into fibroblast growth factor–driven programs, thereby promoting vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and survival. Its membrane topology and ER residency position it as a hub that transiently interfaces with organelle contact sites while primarily executing its scaffolding role at the ER membrane.

A secreted scorpion venom peptide that immobilizes prey by binding and disabling membrane ion channels and transporters in the extracellular milieu. It suppresses excitability by inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels and inwardly rectifying potassium channels, thereby reducing action potential propagation and promoting systemic paralysis. The same binding mechanism plausibly constrains calcium flux indirectly, aligning with its role as a soluble extracellular toxin that enforces negative regulation of channel activity in other organisms.

A secreted venom inhibitory peptide that acts outside cells to suppress calcium channel conductance in target organisms. By binding and dampening membrane channel activity, it reduces calcium influx and perturbs downstream signaling pathways that govern secretion and cytoskeletal dynamics. This primary electrophysiological blockade likely propagates into broader defensive effects characteristic of envenomation, contributing to antimicrobial and antifungal outcomes in the extracellular environment.

A secreted venom-derived peptide from dwarf wood scorpion that adopts a disulfide-stabilized extracellular fold to exert potent toxin activity. It binds and inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels, suppressing excitability in target cells. By paralyzing prey and deterring predators, it serves a broader defensive role and, through direct and indirect antimicrobial actions characteristic of venom peptides, contributes to organismal defense against fungi and bacteria. Its stability and binding surface are tuned for high-affinity interactions in extracellular fluids.

A secreted venom-derived peptide that acts outside cells to exert hormone-like effects on excitable tissues. It suppresses potassium-current pathways by directly inhibiting Kv2.1 and Kv2.2 channel activities and by lowering their surface abundance, thereby dampening excitability in target organisms. This extracellular mode of action aligns with a venom hormone strategy that modulates ion-channel function through high-affinity binding and trafficking control.

A single-pass membrane ligand that presents a DSL module and a calcium-stabilized array of EGF repeats to bind and activate Notch at the cell surface. By anchoring within glycolipid-rich membrane microdomains and undergoing endocytic cycling, it triggers Notch-dependent signaling that governs stem-cell maintenance, asymmetric division, and diverse developmental patterning in imaginal discs and neural lineages. Its extracellular scaffold and trafficking itinerary position it at apical membrane domains and endosomal pathways, where it coordinates fate specification and morphogenesis.

A Ca2+-regulated peripheral membrane scaffold that binds acidic phospholipids and organizes membrane curvature and adhesion during endocytic and phagocytic pathways. By cycling between a cytoplasmic pool and endosomal membranes in response to Ca2+, it assembles oligomeric platforms that stabilize budding and engulfment sites and modulate extracellular vesicle dynamics. Its N-terminal regulatory segment tunes assembly and interaction with trafficking and cytoskeletal machinery, thereby coupling calcium signals to membrane remodeling and cargo uptake.

A membrane-proximal small GTPase switch that cycles between GDP- and GTP-bound states to coordinate actin remodeling and membrane trafficking. By assembling effector complexes at the Golgi, endosomes, plasma membrane rafts, and tight junctions, it directs vesicle transport and cytoskeletal dynamics that promote cell migration, proliferation, and survival signaling. Its nucleotide-dependent conformational changes tune receptor and kinase pathways, integrating cues from growth factors and stress signals while restraining apoptotic cascades in specialized cell types.

A secreted mouse serine endopeptidase that adopts the chymotrypsin-like fold and operates outside the cell to cleave peptide bonds within extracellular substrates. By executing tightly controlled proteolysis of peptide hormone precursors and matrix-associated targets, it contributes to hormone maturation and shapes vascular signaling pathways that influence systemic arterial pressure. The enzyme is produced as a zymogen, activated in the extracellular milieu, and uses a catalytic triad to achieve high specificity for basic-residue–rich targets, thereby coupling extracellular protease activity to broader physiological regulation.

A multi-pass membrane uniporter that facilitates bidirectional movement of glucose, fructose, and L-ascorbic acid across the cell surface. Its major facilitator architecture supports high-capacity, low-affinity alternating-access transport, supplying cytosolic pathways that underpin carbohydrate metabolism and vitamin handling. Positioned at the plasma membrane, it adjusts sugar and antioxidant flux to extracellular availability, with trafficking and scaffolding systems likely tuning its surface abundance and transport kinetics.

A cytosolic homodimeric dehydrogenase that initiates the oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway by oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate and reducing NADP+ to NADPH. Its activity supplies reducing power and ribose precursors that sustain glutathione-dependent antioxidant defense, fatty acid and membrane biogenesis, and nucleotide production. This redox hub is especially critical during erythrocyte maturation and broader stress responses, and it likely operates near cytoskeleton-associated structures and membrane-proximal sites where NADPH demand is high.

A secreted mouse serine endopeptidase that is produced as a zymogen and activated to cleave internal peptide bonds in the extracellular space. Its chymotrypsin-like fold organizes a catalytic triad that drives limited proteolysis, enabling maturation and remodeling of extracellular proteins and matrix components. By engaging substrates and regulatory partners through multivalent binding, it executes targeted proteolysis that shapes pericellular signaling and tissue remodeling.

A calcium-responsive, peripheral membrane protein that binds anionic phospholipids and assembles membrane-proximal scaffolds to regulate endocytosis and phagocytosis. Upon calcium elevation, it translocates from the cytoplasm to organelle membranes where it stabilizes membrane curvature and recruits trafficking machinery, thereby coordinating vesicle formation and cargo sorting. Through this membrane-organizing role and its characteristic N-terminal regulatory segment, it contributes to anti-inflammatory pathways and innate immune engulfment.

A large arenavirus polymerase that unites an N-terminal cap-snatching endonuclease with a central RNA-directed RNA polymerase to coordinate viral transcription and genome replication. It assembles cytoplasmic replication factories that associate with endoplasmic reticulum membranes, where it binds viral and host factors to cleave host capped RNAs for primer acquisition and then synthesizes viral RNAs. By coupling primer theft to RNA synthesis, it drives production of subgenomic transcripts and supports efficient replication of the negative-sense RNA genome.

A soluble signaling enzyme in fission yeast that assembles large cytoplasmic complexes to synthesize cyclic AMP. It integrates inputs from heterotrimeric G-protein and Ras-family pathways through dedicated binding modules and a leucine-rich scaffold, and then uses a C-terminal cyclase core to generate cAMP that drives nutrient-responsive signaling and growth control. Metal coordination within a regulatory fold stabilizes activity, enabling precise modulation of cyclic nucleotide production in the cytoplasm.

A cytosolic 3′→5′ DNA helicase that uses an ATP-driven UvrD-like motor to unwind duplex DNA and remodel replication–repair assemblies. By coupling nucleotide hydrolysis to directional translocation, it clears bound proteins and resolves short duplexes during damage tolerance and repair, thereby supporting postreplication pathways and UV-damage responses within methylation-sensitive DNA transactions.

A calcium-dependent cell-adhesion receptor that assembles adherens junctions and signaling hubs at the cell surface. Its extracellular cadherin ectodomain binds calcium to rigidify adhesion interfaces and drive homophilic clustering, while the cytoplasmic tail recruits catenins and additional adaptors to couple adhesion to the actin cytoskeleton and intracellular pathways. Through this junctional scaffold, it stabilizes epithelial and neuroepithelial contacts, modulates MAPK and Wnt signaling, and coordinates membrane trafficking and synaptic organization. It localizes to apical and apicolateral membranes, raft microdomains, adherens junctions, and specialized muscle and neuronal membranes, where it tunes junction assembly, cell migration, and tissue morphogenesis.

A single-pass cell-surface receptor in mouse that presents an N-terminal glycosaminoglycan-binding ectodomain to capture hyaluronan and extracellular cytokines, thereby organizing higher-order receptor complexes that regulate adhesion, matrix remodeling, and signal transduction. By clustering at the external face of the plasma membrane and coupling to endocytic and kinase pathways, it modulates cytokine and TGF-beta receptor systems, tunes ERK and other phosphorylation cascades, and shapes epithelial morphogenesis and immune responses across basolateral and apical membrane territories and microvillar specializations.

A single-pass cell-surface receptor that uses an N-terminal hyaluronan-binding module to anchor cells to extracellular matrix and to assemble signaling complexes that coordinate adhesion, migration, and immune responses. By clustering at the plasma membrane and within protrusive and adhesive structures, it modulates cytokine-responsive pathways and ERK signaling, thereby promoting leukocyte interactions and T cell activation, guiding wound-associated cell spreading, and influencing tissue morphogenesis and cartilage-related programs. Its trafficking through the secretory pathway and incorporation into vesicles support dynamic localization across the cell surface and polarized membrane domains.

A cell-surface inhibitory receptor on human lymphocytes that uses an extracellular immunoglobulin-like module to bind a counter-receptor on antigen-presenting cells, thereby attenuating T-cell activation and effector responses. It resides on the external face of the plasma membrane and traffics through the secretory and endocytic systems, where it assembles with adhesion-related complexes and undergoes clathrin-mediated internalization. By coupling ligand-induced endocytosis with inhibitory signaling, it curtails immune receptor pathways, promotes apoptotic programs in specific contexts, and modulates regulatory T-cell differentiation and broader lymphocyte and B-cell signaling.

A soluble cytoplasmic enzyme that uses ATP-coupled citrate and CoA chemistry to generate acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate, thereby supplying the acetyl units required for cytosolic lipid and sterol biosynthesis. Its multi-domain architecture binds citrate, ATP, and CoA, executes sequential phosphoryl and acyl-transfer steps characteristic of citrate/citrate–CoA lyase families, and channels acetyl-CoA toward fatty acid and broader acetyl-CoA–dependent pathways in the cytoplasm.

A secreted venom metalloprotease that is produced as a zymogen and activated by prodomain removal to expose a zinc-dependent catalytic core. It operates in the extracellular space where its catalytic module cleaves target proteins while a C‑terminal disintegrin appendage targets integrin-rich platelet and vascular surfaces. Through coupled proteolysis and adhesive targeting, it suppresses platelet adhesion and aggregation and broadly dampens hemostatic pathways in envenomed organisms.

A Ca2+-regulated membrane-organizing scaffold that assembles at the cell surface and vesicles to control membrane dynamics and local calcium signaling. By binding acidic phospholipids in a calcium-dependent manner, it oligomerizes into surface lattices that recruit trafficking machinery and can stabilize or form calcium-permeable conduits. This coordination of membrane remodeling and calcium flux supports cytokine production and gene regulation, and drives tissue-specific programs including bone and cartilage mineralization, endocardial and endothelial differentiation, and matrix-associated protease pathways. It operates at the plasma membrane, vesicles, and extracellular matrix interfaces as part of larger calcium-handling assemblies.

A stress-gated bZIP transcription factor that shuttles between an endoplasmic reticulum–tethered pool and the nucleus to coordinate unfolded protein response gene programs. It dimerizes through its basic leucine zipper to bind specific promoter elements, recruits transcriptional cofactors, and modulates chromatin to regulate RNA polymerase II–dependent transcription. By coupling ER stress sensing to nuclear gene expression, it orchestrates proteostasis and ER-associated degradation, tunes autophagy and proteasome pathways, and broadly impacts immune, vascular, and signaling networks through regulated nucleocytoplasmic transport and membrane-associated assembly.

A soluble adaptor that orchestrates the desensitization and internalization of membrane receptors. It binds activated receptor cytoplasmic tails and, upon membrane and phosphate-sensing cues, exposes motifs that recruit clathrin and associated endocytic machinery. This assembly terminates G protein coupling, promotes receptor endocytosis at coated pits, and directs cargo through cytoplasmic vesicle pathways. Its bilobal scaffold coordinates lipid and phosphate interactions to switch between signaling and endocytic states, thereby coupling receptor desensitization to vesicular trafficking.

A type I membrane glycoprotein in mouse whose large immunoglobulin-like ectodomain mediates multivalent protein binding to organize adhesive and signaling assemblies at the cell surface. By scaffolding membrane-protein networks, it supports photoreceptor maintenance and retinal development and likely contributes to germ cell maturation. It localizes to the plasma membrane and is enriched in photoreceptor inner and outer segments; in male germ cells it associates with the acrosomal membrane. Its mechanism centers on extracellular adhesion via Ig-like domains coupled to intracellular adaptor recruitment that tunes vesicle trafficking and membrane remodeling.

A single-pass cell-surface adhesion receptor that uses a calcium-stabilized extracellular cadherin module to mediate homophilic cell-cell adhesion and a cytoplasmic tail to recruit catenins and couple junctions to the actin cytoskeleton. By assembling a catenin complex at adherens junctions, it stabilizes cortical actin, supports lamellipodial and focal adhesion dynamics, and transmits mechanical cues that underlie responses to muscle stretch. Its biosynthesis and maturation traverse the secretory pathway, and its junctional assemblies interface with the collagen-rich extracellular matrix.

A Ca2+-regulated, membrane-associated scaffold that binds anionic phospholipids upon Ca2+ elevation and organizes endocytic and exocytic membrane platforms. By assembling Ca2+-responsive complexes at early endosomes and the cell surface, it modulates membrane dynamics and local Ca2+ handling, thereby tuning vesicle trafficking and Ca2+ flux pathways that feed into anti-inflammatory signaling and membrane remodeling.

A type III intermediate filament subunit that assembles into a resilient cytoplasmic filament network essential for neuronal and glial architecture and for lens fiber cell maturation. Its N-terminal head domain mediates nucleic acid and protein interactions that regulate filament assembly and RNA-associated granules, while the central coiled-coil rod drives filament formation and stability. By scaffolding signaling and RNA-processing modules at cortical and vesicle-rich regions, it organizes intermediate filament networks that support neuron and astrocyte development, restrain excessive neurite outgrowth, and couple cytoskeletal architecture to SMAD-dependent transcription and interferon-responsive pathways.

A single-pass cell-surface adhesion receptor that forms a heterodimer with β integrins to mediate high-affinity binding to counter-receptors and extracellular matrix, thereby coordinating cell adhesion with intracellular signaling. Its extracellular β-propeller and adhesion module capture ligands and transmit mechanical cues, while a short cytoplasmic tail assembles signaling complexes that potentiate kinase pathways. This coupling drives adhesion-dependent programs including cell–cell cohesion, migration, proliferation, and angiogenic remodeling, with regulated trafficking through specialized granules tuning surface availability in vascular and hematopoietic contexts.

A cytosolic, membrane-recruited signaling scaffold and GTPase-activating factor that uses tandem phosphotyrosine-recognition modules to dock onto phosphorylated receptor complexes, membrane-targeting elements to stabilize at phosphoinositide-rich sites, and a catalytic core to accelerate GTP hydrolysis on small GTPases. By coupling receptor-proximal recruitment with actin-regulatory GTPase control, it dampens receptor-driven pathways, modulates adhesion and cytoskeletal dynamics, and supports morphogenetic programs and cell survival.

A soluble RNA-binding regulator that coats poly(A) tails through tandem RNA-recognition motifs and uses a C-terminal interaction hub to assemble translation and mRNA-turnover complexes. By stabilizing and organizing the 3′ end of transcripts and recruiting initiation machinery, it enhances translation and coordinates nuclear splicing with cytoplasmic mRNA fate. This coupling of RNA binding and assembly functions supports germline and developmental programs, neuronal survival and signaling, and precise control of gene expression in both cytoplasm and nucleus.

A soluble alpha-subunit enzyme that assembles into a higher-order catalytic particle responsible for hydrating nitriles to amide/amine products in actinobacteria. Its conserved alpha/γ fold drives multimerization and builds the active-site environment of a soluble complex that advances cellular pathways handling nitrogen-containing substrates. Operating as part of a catalytic assembly rather than a membrane anchor, it supports nitrile detoxification and assimilation through assembly-coupled chemistry in the bacterial cytosol.

A soluble beta subunit of a cytosolic nitrile hydratase that assembles and stabilizes the multimeric enzyme complex responsible for converting nitriles to amides. It provides the structural scaffold that organizes and tunes the catalytic alpha subunits, enabling water addition to nitriles and channeling products into downstream nitrogen-catabolic pathways. Operating in the cytoplasm, it achieves function through extensive protein–protein interfaces that build the active holoenzyme and coordinate flux through nitrile detoxification and assimilation routes.

A membrane-associated heterotrimeric GTP-binding switch that couples activated receptors to phospholipase C signaling. By cycling between GDP- and GTP-bound states, it dissociates from the beta–gamma dimer and directly stimulates phospholipase C to produce IP3 and DAG, elevating intracellular calcium and PKC activity. This signaling cascade regulates calcium channels and other ion-conducting pathways, shaping postsynaptic transmission, endocrine secretion, cardiovascular tone, pigmentation pathways, and organismal development and aging. The complex operates at the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane as part of the heterotrimeric G-protein assembly.

A soluble serine/threonine protein kinase of the ERK branch of the MAPK pathway that binds ATP and phosphorylates proline-directed sites on target proteins to transmit mitogenic and stress signals. By shuttling between cytoplasm and nucleus, it modulates transcriptional and cytoskeletal programs that shape developmental morphogenesis, including structures formed during oogenesis. Activation by upstream dual phosphorylation and action on downstream transcription factors and cytoskeletal regulators provide a mechanism for controlling gene expression and cell architecture that together drive morphogenetic outcomes.

An erythrocyte-adhesion protein in Plasmodium vivax that assembles multivalent binding platforms to anchor merozoites to red blood cells. Its modular adhesion architecture promotes homooligomerization and high-avidity attachment at membrane-proximal sites, initiating invasion and contributing to parasite strategies that suppress replication within infected erythrocytes. By stabilizing host–parasite membrane contacts and clustering adhesion sites, it supports processes that indirectly counter viral propagation in the erythrocytic niche.

A soluble mitochondrial flavoprotein that uses a FAD/NADP-binding core to accept reducing power from NADPH and deliver single electrons to an iron–sulfur ferredoxin. By sustaining the reduced ferredoxin pool, it energizes mitochondrial monooxygenase systems that drive steroid hormone biosynthesis. Operating on the matrix-facing side of the organelle, it forms transient assemblies with ferredoxin and inner-membrane enzymes to relay electrons through a dedicated pathway that links cellular reducing equivalents to steroidogenic chemistry.

An atypical seven-transmembrane chemokine receptor that binds C-C chemokines with high affinity at the cell surface and then internalizes them through endocytic pathways. By capturing and clearing chemokines and routing them through vesicles and endosomes, it reshapes extracellular gradients and indirectly enhances chemotaxis. The receptor cycles between the plasma membrane and intracellular compartments, with soluble pools in the cytoplasm and occasional nuclear-associated fractions, reflecting a trafficking-centric mechanism rather than classical G-protein signaling.

A multi-pass membrane transporter in baker’s yeast that uses a major facilitator architecture to shuttle carbohydrate derivatives and organophosphate esters across biological membranes. It likely harnesses the proton motive force to drive alternating-access transport at the cell surface and the vacuolar membrane, thereby balancing cytosolic pools of phosphorylated sugars and related metabolites. By cycling between the plasma membrane and the fungal vacuole, it contributes to broader transmembrane transport programs that couple nutrient exchange with storage and detoxification pathways.

A plasma membrane, multi-pass anion transporter in baker’s yeast that uses an N-terminal regulatory sensor to tune phosphate-coupled transport through a C-terminal membrane core. By coupling phosphate-rich ligand sensing to secondary active translocation, it mediates and modulates phosphate exchange across the cell surface, thereby coordinating phosphate homeostasis with polyphosphate turnover and broader anion and organic acid metabolism.

A papain-like cysteine endopeptidase that is synthesized as a zymogen with an autoinhibitory prodomain and activated in acidic compartments to drive proteolysis central to intracellular and extracellular turnover. It contributes to bulk protein degradation and peptide generation, remodels extracellular matrix by binding and cleaving matrix components, and supports antigen processing and immune signaling within endolysosomal pathways. The enzyme traffics through endosomes and lysosomes, can be secreted to act in the extracellular space and collagen-rich matrices, and likely coordinates with acidic pH–dependent activation to couple matrix remodeling with immune-related peptide handling.

A signal-responsive transcriptional regulator that integrates immune and stress cues through an N-terminal DNA-binding and dimerization engine coupled to a C-terminal regulatory tail. It resides predominantly in the cytoplasm under basal conditions and translocates to the nucleus upon activation, where processed forms assemble with partner subunits to control RNA polymerase II–dependent gene programs. By binding κB DNA elements and recruiting chromatin-associated cofactors, it modulates cytokine and antiviral pathways, shapes inflammatory tone, and coordinates broader developmental and stress-responsive transcriptional networks.

A single-pass thylakoid membrane redox subunit that forms the iron–sulfur catalytic head of the cytochrome b6-f complex in cyanobacteria. Anchored in the thylakoid membrane, it uses a Rieske-type [2Fe-2S] center to shuttle single electrons between adjacent redox partners within the complex, thereby coupling plastoquinol oxidation to downstream electron flow that drives ATP formation. Its membrane-tethered headpiece alternates docking with neighboring subunits to gate electron transfer and sustain the photosynthetic electron transport chain.

A receptor-proximal serine/threonine kinase in cattle that assembles with activated G protein-coupled receptors via an N-terminal receptor-docking module and a membrane-targeting tail to phosphorylate receptor cytoplasmic regions. This phosphorylation drives receptor desensitization and endocytic internalization, thereby dampening signaling through adrenergic and cholinergic pathways. By tuning receptor output, it modulates cell-to-cell communication and muscle physiology, including cardiac contraction and its force control, and it can influence membrane-associated signaling assemblies through transient cytosolic and membrane-localized cycles.

A nucleocytoplasmic serine/threonine protein kinase that operates as a central node in receptor- and stress-activated signaling. It binds ATP and transfers phosphate via a mitogen-activated kinase core, assembling transient complexes that propagate signals from membrane microdomains and endocytic routes to the nucleus. By docking transcription factors and regulatory enzymes, it modulates gene expression, cytoskeletal dynamics, endocytosis, and organelle organization. Its shuttling between cytosol and nucleoplasm enables control of proliferation, survival, and differentiation programs, with endosomal and Golgi-associated assemblies tuning pathway amplitude and duration.

A nucleocytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase that executes mitogen-activated signaling to control cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Its ERK-class architecture supports ATP-dependent phosphorylation of numerous substrates, enabling rapid cytoplasmic responses and stimulus-triggered nuclear translocation to regulate transcriptional programs. By shuttling between cytoplasm and nucleus and using scaffolded assemblies and phosphatase feedback, it channels extracellular cues into morphogenetic outputs relevant to developmental patterning.

A soluble adaptor that cycles between cytoplasm and plasma membrane to terminate and reprogram receptor signaling. It binds activated, phosphorylated receptors and assembles endocytic and signaling modules, driving clathrin-mediated internalization and early endosomal sorting. By diverting and attenuating receptor-driven pathways, it suppresses ERK cascade output and coordinates adhesion and migration programs, with prominent activity in dendritic neuronal compartments.

A soluble α-subunit of a nitrile-hydrating enzyme in Rhodococcus that assembles into a higher-order complex to initiate aerobic nitrile detoxification. By forming an oligomeric particle that positions a catalytic environment for hydratase chemistry, it converts nitriles to amides that feed downstream nitrogen-catabolic routes. Its role depends on multivalent assembly with partner subunits and maturation factors, operating as a cytosolic enzyme-complex hub that channels diverse nitriles into central metabolism.

A cytosolic beta subunit of a heterotrimeric nitrile hydratase that organizes and stabilizes the enzyme complex responsible for converting nitriles to amides in Rhodococcus. It does not carry the catalytic cysteine but provides a bipartite scaffold that binds the catalytic partner, tunes active-site geometry, and supports assembly and allosteric control. By enabling efficient hydratase function, it feeds nitrile detoxification into cellular nitrogen breakdown pathways within the cytoplasm.

A cytosolic ATP-dependent ligase that assembles the D-alanine–D-alanine dipeptide and can also generate D-alanine–L-alanine, thereby sustaining the pools of cell-wall precursors used in peptidoglycan biogenesis. Its two-lobed ATP-grasp architecture binds and activates ATP and metal ions to drive amide-bond formation, supplying building blocks that indirectly tune stress pathways and maintain envelope integrity in Gram-positive cells.

A membrane-proximal heterotrimeric GTPase that transduces signals from seven-transmembrane receptors to intracellular pathways. It cycles between GDP- and GTP-bound states to control assembly with partner subunits and effectors, thereby activating phospholipase C–dependent cascades and propagating calcium- and PKC-based signaling. Its switch mechanism and partner-binding surfaces position it near cellular membranes, including endolysosomal sites, where it coordinates receptor-triggered signal flow.

A seven-helix membrane receptor that detects extracellular adenosine and converts this signal into intracellular responses by coupling to heterotrimeric G proteins. Its multi-pass architecture at the cell surface enables ligand-triggered conformational changes that engage Gi/o pathways and associated scaffolds, reshaping second messenger and kinase networks. Through this mechanism it mediates intercellular communication, modulates inflammatory and apoptotic signaling, and influences neural development and phagocytic programs.

A cytoplasmic intermediate filament scaffold that assembles into 10-nm filaments to provide mechanical support and organize signaling in neurons and glia. Its head–rod–tail architecture drives filament formation and multivalent binding surfaces that recruit kinases, phosphatases, and adhesion-associated adaptors. By stabilizing perinuclear and axonal networks and coordinating phosphorylation-dependent remodeling, it supports cell differentiation and growth, integrates hormone and growth factor responses, and contributes to axonogenesis, glial proliferation and migration, and tissue regeneration.

A soluble acyl-CoA–binding protein in baker’s yeast that uses a compact acyl-CoA–binding fold to sequester and deliver very long-chain acyl-CoA thioesters. By buffering and channeling these reactive intermediates, it promotes elongation and assembly of very long-chain lipids in the cytoplasm, with potential shuttling to the nucleus for lipid-responsive regulation and occasional release outside the cell.
