Its bilobal kinase core binds ATP and transfers phosphate via a conserved catalytic loop, enabling broad substrate scope and stable control over gene-regulatory pathways.

A multi-pass plasma membrane transporter in mouse that uses an alternating-access mechanism to move hydrophobic thyroid hormones and related small molecules across the cell surface. By cycling between inward- and outward-facing states, it modulates intracellular pools of thyroid hormone and likely contributes to broader hormone and metabolite handling, including steroid and bile acid pathways as well as uptake and efflux of diverse drugs and endogenous hydrophobes.

A soluble adaptor that forms a dimeric clamp to bind phosphorylated client proteins and remodel their conformations, thereby tuning signaling, cell-cycle control, and apoptosis. It operates primarily in the cytoplasm but also shuttles to the nucleus with its cargo. By stabilizing specific conformations and assembling higher-order complexes, it promotes kinase pathway output and orchestrates phosphorylation-dependent regulation across diverse cellular pathways.

A single-pass cell-surface receptor-like protein in human ovarian tissue that presents a large calcium-tuned ectodomain to capture extracellular ligands and matrix components, then undergoes pH-triggered release during endocytic trafficking. By clustering and internalizing specific cues at the plasma membrane, it modulates signaling pathways that govern follicular maturation and the progression of oocyte development, thereby contributing to germ cell and oogenesis pathways.

A human multi-pass membrane transporter that uses a major facilitator mechanism to move neutral and aromatic amino acids across the cell surface. It mediates transmembrane flux of isoleucine, leucine, valine, phenylalanine, histidine, and alanine, thereby sustaining cellular amino acid supply and signaling. Its fold and ion-coupled alternating-access cycle position it at the plasma membrane, where it integrates gradient energy to drive uptake and redistribution of branched-chain and aromatic amino acids.

A soluble human oxidoreductase that resides predominantly in the cytoplasm and uses a nicotinamide-dependent short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase fold to interconvert retinol and retinaldehyde, thereby controlling retinoid pools and extending its chemistry to isatin and its aldehyde product. By tuning cytosolic retinoid balance and processing related carbonyl substrates, it supports pathways that feed into vision. Its soluble architecture and cofactor-binding core drive reversible hydride transfer, positioning the enzyme as a hub for cytoplasmic retinoid and isatin metabolism with occasional extracellular detection likely via vesicle-mediated export or soluble leakage.

A soluble nicotinamide-dependent oxidoreductase in cattle that remodels the redox state of hydrophobic steroid and bile acid intermediates. It uses a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase catalytic center to interconvert alcohol and ketone groups on 3α- and 7α-hydroxysteroids, thereby tuning glucocorticoid and broader steroid pathways. Operating in the cytoplasm and functionally coupled to the endoplasmic reticulum, it likely accesses membrane-associated steroid pools and transiently assembles with ER-proximal enzymes to balance hormone and bile acid metabolism through stereospecific hydride transfer chemistry.

A nuclear transcriptional regulator that assembles as a higher-order complex to control gene expression programs central to epithelial differentiation and cell-fate decisions. It uses a central site-specific DNA-recognition module to bind target elements, a tetramerization core to stabilize cooperative promoter occupancy, and a C-terminal interaction hub to recruit chromatin-modifying cofactors. Through these multivalent assemblies, it activates transcriptional networks that govern epithelial lineage functions and influence tumorigenesis and tumor suppressor pathways.

An inner-membrane–associated, matrix-facing ATP-dependent zinc metalloprotease in mouse mitochondria that couples an AAA+ unfoldase/translocase to a proteolytic chamber to extract, disassemble, and degrade misfolded or unassembled proteins. By using ATP hydrolysis to drive polypeptide threading and cleavage, it safeguards mitochondrial proteostasis and supports maturation and turnover of inner-membrane and matrix-exposed substrates, thereby sustaining overall mitochondrial function.

A secreted fungal endo-acting glycoside hydrolase that cleaves internal β-1,4 linkages of xylan in the extracellular environment, initiating and accelerating hemicellulose depolymerization. By fragmenting xylan into soluble oligomers that downstream enzymes can fully degrade, it drives extracellular xylan breakdown and nutrient acquisition. Its catalytic core and lectin/glucanase-like scaffold position acidic residues for hydrolytic chemistry, and its extracellular deployment aligns with coordinated action alongside other plant cell wall–degrading enzymes.

A secreted human decoy member of the tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily that uses a cysteine-rich extracellular domain to bind and neutralize pro-apoptotic TNF-family ligands. By sequestering these extracellular cues without an intracellular signaling apparatus, it prevents assembly of death-inducing pathways and thereby dampens apoptosis. Its activity occurs outside the cell, where multivalent binding surfaces capture soluble cytokines and extracellular receptor complexes to suppress apoptotic signaling.

A cytoplasmic actin-assembly factor that uses an N-terminal regulatory scaffold and a C-terminal catalytic core to control filament dynamics. It binds small GTPase modules and associated regulators to relieve autoinhibition, exposing an actin-assembly engine that nucleates and elongates filaments with profilin–actin. By remodeling actin networks at membrane-proximal sites, it supports cell migration and coordinates actin-dependent events at the plasma membrane and phagocytic vesicles.

A large human nuclear scaffold that uses an extended MYM-type zinc-finger array and a C-terminal nucleic-acid–engaging fold to assemble regulatory complexes controlling cell shape and cytoskeletal organization. By concentrating multivalent protein–protein interactions in the nucleus, it likely coordinates chromatin- and RNA-associated assemblies that tune expression and trafficking of cytoskeletal regulators, thereby coupling nuclear programs to cytoskeletal dynamics and cell morphogenesis.

A soluble human pyrophosphohydrolase that resides in the cytosol and hydrolyzes pyrophosphate bonds in nucleoside diphosphate–linked metabolites. By using a metal-dependent catalytic core to regulate nucleotide-derived signaling molecules, it stabilizes cytosolic metabolite pools and indirectly supports the efficiency of co-translational targeting and endoplasmic reticulum–dependent N-linked glycosylation. Its soluble architecture and catalytic chemistry position it as a cytosolic regulator that conditions glycoprotein biogenesis pathways.

A secreted and membrane-associated extracellular regulator that assembles a cysteine-rich scaffold to bind matrix and cell-surface receptors while suppressing pericellular proteolysis. Its modular architecture concentrates and inhibits protease systems at the cell surface, thereby stabilizing adhesion, restraining cell migration, and promoting differentiation cues consistent with tumor-suppressive activity. By organizing extracellular interactions and dampening metalloproteinase-driven matrix remodeling, it modulates signaling pathways that govern cell fate and invasion.

A Golgi-localized, single-pass type II membrane enzyme that couples N-deacetylation of glucosamine residues with sulfate transfer onto heparan sulfate chains during proteoglycan biosynthesis. Its N-terminal deacetylase module exposes amino groups on the polymer, and its C-terminal sulfotransferase core installs sulfate esters using a nucleotide-sulfate donor. By coordinating these sequential reactions in the Golgi lumen, it establishes key sulfation patterns that shape heparan sulfate structure and function.

A soluble enzyme that hydrolyzes acyl phosphate bonds and thereby shapes cellular phosphate and energy metabolism. It forms a compact catalytic scaffold that likely homodimerizes to stabilize its active site and efficiently detoxify reactive acyl phosphate intermediates. The enzyme predominantly operates in the cytoplasm, with potential association near plastid-linked pathways that account for a chloroplast-related annotation. Its mechanism centers on a conserved catalytic site that stabilizes a pentavalent transition state to cleave phosphorus-containing anhydrides.

A secreted prohormone that is proteolytically processed into two bioactive nonapeptides that act as neuropeptide hormones. After folding and disulfide stabilization, the matured peptides bind a neuropeptide-responsive receptor to initiate G protein–coupled signaling that elevates intracellular second messengers and modulates endocrine secretion, including stimulation of insulin release. This extracellular signaling axis secondarily engages intracellular kinase pathways and survival programs that temper apoptotic protease activity.

A secreted human prohormone that is proteolytically processed into a neuropeptide hormone and an associated peptide, acting as a high-affinity extracellular ligand that activates its cognate receptor to drive intercellular signaling. By engaging G protein–coupled pathways, it stimulates kinase and MAPK/PKC cascades, enhances serine phosphorylation and gene-expression programs, and promotes epithelial water handling while suppressing apoptotic machinery. Its cystine-stabilized secretory architecture ensures proper folding and trafficking through the regulated secretory pathway, culminating in extracellular action that coordinates systemic water balance and cell survival.

A secreted neuroendocrine prohormone that is proteolytically processed into two bioactive nonapeptides that act as potent endocrine ligands. After folding and disulfide-bond stabilization, the mature peptides bind their cognate G protein–coupled receptor to trigger intracellular kinase-driven signaling and vesicle exocytosis pathways. This signaling enhances insulin release from pancreatic islet cells and broadly modulates neurocrine outputs, with downstream effects that include suppression of apoptotic cascades through reduced caspase activation.

A soybean seed storage globulin that assembles a stable cupin-based trimer to accumulate amino acids and nitrogen during seed development. It is synthesized through the secretory pathway, undergoes conserved maturation, and forms homotrimers that pack into higher-order storage particles characteristic of seed storage bodies. By providing a durable reservoir of nutrients, it supports late embryogenesis and post-embryonic energy balance, accumulating outside the cytosol as part of secretory-derived storage compartments.

A soybean seed storage protein that assembles a stable cupin-based oligomer to sequester amino acids and nitrogen during seed filling and later remobilization. It enters the secretory pathway, undergoes maturation, and is deposited into extracellularized seed reserves where its exceptional stability supports nutrient storage. The exposed β-barrel surfaces that drive oligomerization also present conformational epitopes that can bind IgE, explaining its allergenic behavior. Through this architecture, it contributes critically to seed maturation and energy reserve accumulation.

A legumin-type seed storage protein in soybean that assembles a stable cupin-based oligomer to sequester amino acids and nitrogen during seed development. Its jelly-roll scaffold promotes homotrimer formation and durable storage-body assembly, channeling reserves that support seed maturation and later mobilization during germination. Synthesized through the secretory pathway and deposited into extracellular-facing seed compartments, it functions as a nutrient reservoir whose robust architecture ensures long-term stability under desiccation.

A soybean seed storage protein that accumulates as a highly stable reservoir of amino acids and nitrogen during late embryogenesis. It is synthesized through the secretory pathway and assembles into multimeric complexes that protect and concentrate nutrients until germination. Its cupin-based scaffold drives robust oligomerization and resistance to degradation, enabling it to support seed maturation and long-term viability within extracellular/secretory routes that deliver it to storage depots.

A single-pass cell-surface adhesion receptor that forms an obligate heterodimer with alpha integrins to anchor cells to extracellular matrix and transmit bidirectional signals. Its extracellular head binds matrix ligands and organizes growth factor and chemokine cues, while a cysteine-rich stalk and short cytoplasmic tail couple to cytoskeletal and kinase assemblies. This architecture enables strong cell–matrix adhesion, platelet and vascular signaling, synaptic receptor trafficking, and broad adhesion-dependent pathways at lamellipodia, ruffles, and focal adhesions. By clustering with growth factor and receptor systems, it acts as a coreceptor that elevates and routes signaling outputs across diverse physiological processes.

A calcium- and diacylglycerol-gated serine/threonine kinase that integrates second-messenger signals to control apoptosis, differentiation, and cytoskeletal remodeling. It is recruited to membranes by lipid- and calcium-binding modules and then phosphorylates diverse substrates to modulate transcriptional and chromatin-associated pathways, cell shape, and motility. Its signaling stabilizes client proteins by dampening ubiquitination and proteolysis and can enhance DNA repair pathways. The enzyme cycles between the plasma membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus, where it assembles with partners to orchestrate phosphorylation cascades.

A soluble neuroendocrine precursor that enters the secretory pathway and accumulates in secretory granules, where it binds partners and nucleotides to chaperone and organize peptide-hormone cargo. By stabilizing sorting and maturation assemblies, it promotes orderly intracellular transport and processing of prohormones, thereby tuning the efficiency and timing of hormone secretion from dense-core vesicles.

A classical, calcium- and diacylglycerol-activated serine/threonine kinase that assembles at DAG-enriched membranes via tandem lipid/Ca2+-sensing modules and then phosphorylates cytosolic and nuclear substrates to coordinate secretion and transcriptional programs. It cycles between the plasma membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus, where it modulates vesicle-associated pathways and gene-expression machinery. By coupling membrane recruitment to catalytic activation through AGC-family regulatory elements, it orchestrates hormone release and broader signaling networks that tune cellular responses.

A calcium- and diacylglycerol-regulated serine/threonine kinase that cycles between cytosol and membranes to control signaling assemblies. Its N-terminal lipid-sensing modules recruit the enzyme to DAG-enriched membrane microdomains, where a conserved AGC kinase core phosphorylates targets that govern apoptosis, differentiation, and cytoskeletal organization. By docking onto scaffolded complexes and PDZ-containing assemblies, it amplifies GPCR-driven pathways that stimulate adenylate cyclase signaling. Dynamic localization to cytosol, brush border membranes, and centrosomes supports coordinated control of membrane-proximal and cytoskeletal processes.

A lentiviral accessory adaptor that uses a compact interaction scaffold to assemble host–viral complexes central to infection. By binding soluble transport machinery and nuclear pore components, it accumulates in the host nucleus, where it modulates nuclear transport and proteostasis to sustain the viral life cycle and blunt apoptosis. Its mechanism is non-enzymatic: multivalent protein binding that redirects host pathways governing cell-cycle control and cell death, thereby promoting productive replication and survival of the infected cell.

A soluble lentiviral accessory factor that accumulates in the cytoplasm and shuttles to the nucleus of infected cells. It functions as a multivalent adaptor that binds other proteins to drive assembly and maturation of the viral capsid and to remodel host pathways that favor late-stage replication. By organizing transient complexes in the cytoplasm and engaging nuclear transport and chromatin-associated systems, it coordinates late steps of virion assembly with nuclear functions essential for productive infection.

A cell-surface adhesion receptor that forms an αβ heterodimer to mediate high-affinity attachment to extracellular matrix ligands such as fibronectin. Its extracellular β-propeller head and immunoglobulin-like stalk create a mechanically responsive ectodomain that binds matrix, while a short cytoplasmic tail couples to intracellular adaptors to regulate activation and signaling. Through this bidirectional signaling, it stabilizes cell–matrix adhesion and modulates pathways that adjust migration and growth in response to nitric oxide, operating as a single-pass type I membrane component of the integrin complex at the plasma membrane and cell surface.

A lentiviral accessory adaptor that forms homodimers and higher-order assemblies to coordinate cytoplasmic stages of virion production. It scaffolds capsid assembly and packaging, associates with capsid-proximal structures inside virions, and operates in the host cytoplasm where assembly initiates. By clustering with viral and host partners, it likely bridges capsid intermediates to transport and repair pathways, thereby coupling virion assembly with intracellular trafficking and genome-maintenance functions.

A heme-binding β-type scaffold of the cyanobacterial antenna complex that assembles and stabilizes the phycobilisome to funnel excitation energy toward photosystem II. Its globin-like fold coordinates a structural heme, enforcing precise subunit geometry and chromophore alignment that optimize energy transfer. By organizing this supramolecular assembly in the cytoplasmic compartment where it is synthesized and assembled, it supports photosynthetic energy harvesting and indirectly couples to broader metabolic pathways, including vitamin and cofactor biosynthesis.

A soluble phosphocarrier that drives the central phosphorylation cycle of the bacterial sugar-uptake pathway by transiently binding partner proteins and switching between histidine- and serine-phosphorylated states. This reversible scaffold receives phosphate from Enzyme I and donates it to membrane-associated uptake modules, thereby tuning carbon flux and coordinating with envelope biogenesis pathways. Through this coupling, it operates predominantly in the cytoplasm while functionally engaging membrane and cell wall interfaces, where its regulatory influence on metabolic and surface programs can dampen pathways that stabilize blood–pathogen interactions.

A soluble dimeric oxidoreductase in chicken that couples a cytochrome b5-like heme module to a molybdenum-cofactor catalytic core to oxidize sulfur-bearing substrates. By relaying electrons from the heme-bearing N-terminus into the central redox center and stabilizing the active dimer via a C-terminal scaffold, it supports cytosolic and nuclear pools of redox activity that feed into broader carbon-utilization pathways.

A secreted human serine endopeptidase that is produced as a latent zymogen and activated outside the cell to remodel the pericellular environment. Its trypsin-like catalytic core drives peptide-bond cleavage that promotes hemostatic signaling, while affinity for heparin-like glycans concentrates the enzyme at injured surfaces. By assembling transient complexes with other proteases and receptors, it can act as a soluble ligand that enhances clot formation and coordinates extracellular proteolysis central to coagulation.

A single-pass cell-surface adhesion receptor that forms a heterodimer with a beta integrin to mediate high-affinity binding to extracellular ligands and cell-surface partners. Its extracellular beta-propeller head and immunoglobulin-like stalk create a calcium-tuned adhesion platform, while a short cytoplasmic tail transduces outside-in and inside-out signals that assemble and stabilize junctions. Through this bidirectional signaling, it orchestrates cell adhesion and junction assembly in vascular and immune contexts and contributes to neural circuit stabilization linked to memory.

A nuclear transcription regulator that binds palindromic DNA elements through a conserved N‑terminal module and uses a modular interaction surface to assemble transcriptional complexes. It can stimulate RNA polymerase II–dependent transcription when recruiting co-activators, yet also assemble repressive machinery that dampens gene expression. Operating within the nucleus, it toggles between activation and repression by coupling high-affinity DNA anchoring with context-dependent cofactor recruitment.

A diacylglycerol-gated serine/threonine kinase that cycles between cytosolic and membrane-associated pools to coordinate signal-induced phosphorylation with cytoskeletal remodeling and vesicle dynamics. Its N-terminal membrane-targeting modules recruit the catalytic core to DAG-rich membranes where it phosphorylates substrates that tune GPCR-driven pathways, restrain regulated secretion, and dampen calcium flux. By assembling with other enzymes and scaffolds, it both activates downstream effectors and imposes negative control over exocytosis and neurotransmitter release, consistent with roles in cytoskeletal regulation and signal transduction.

A secreted staphylococcal serine endopeptidase that adopts a chymotrypsin-like fold and uses a catalytic histidine–serine apparatus to cleave extracellular epithelial surface proteins, thereby promoting epidermal cell shedding and tissue remodeling. By dismantling adhesion and junctional components at the host surface, it triggers signaling pathways that elevate transcriptional programs associated with wound responses and tissue turnover.

A secreted developmental morphogen that assembles extracellular gradients by binding both cell-surface receptors and sulfated proteoglycans, thereby activating receptor-mediated pathways that pattern the embryo and stimulate proliferative zones. Its cysteine-rich fold and conserved internal site enable high-affinity receptor engagement and matrix tethering, producing positional information that specifies anterior–posterior axes and coordinates with other growth factor pathways in the extracellular space.

A nuclear ADP-ribosyltransferase that senses DNA damage and hypoxic stress, binds to damaged chromatin through specialized zinc fingers and nucleic-acid–binding modules, and rapidly polymerizes ADP-ribose onto nearby proteins and histones. This transient PARylation remodels chromatin and repair assemblies, enabling assembly and turnover of DNA-repair and transcriptional complexes. By coupling NAD+-dependent catalysis to chromatin-bound scaffolds, it can both repress and potentiate transcription, with a soluble cytoplasmic pool that supports shuttling and complex assembly.

A soluble bacterial RNA-dependent ATPase that terminates transcription by capturing nascent single-stranded RNA with an N-terminal RNA-binding head and using a C-terminal ATP-driven motor to translocate along the transcript. This energy-coupled translocation destabilizes the elongation complex and releases RNA, producing intrinsic termination independent of signal sequences. The enzyme assembles via homotypic contacts to form an active translocase and operates in the cytoplasm where transcription occurs.

A cytoplasmic antitermination factor that stabilizes elongating transcription complexes and suppresses premature termination during bacterial gene expression. It uses an N-terminal interaction platform to anchor onto the transcription machinery and a C-terminal KOW module that engages RNA and ribosomal surfaces, thereby coupling transcription to translation. Through these coordinated binding events, it promotes readthrough of intrinsic and Rho-dependent termination signals and sustains productive elongation within larger cytosolic assemblies.

A soluble calcium-sensing regulator in human cells that uses EF-hand modules to undergo calcium-triggered conformational changes and bind partner proteins within contractile assemblies. By coupling calcium binding to high-affinity, state-dependent interactions, it stabilizes and modulates the troponin–thin filament system that switches tropomyosin on and off actin, thereby controlling contraction within cytoplasmic myofibrillar structures and concentrating near apical contractile regions.

A virion-localized coronavirus accessory scaffold that oligomerizes to anchor within the particle’s internal matrix, where it binds other viral structural assemblies and transiently engages host factors. Through multivalent binding, it stabilizes virion architecture and assembly while attenuating cytoplasmic pattern-recognition signaling pathways that drive innate immunity. Its mechanism relies on a conserved coronavirus core domain that promotes matrix association and complex formation rather than catalysis.

A cytoplasmic zinc-stabilized inhibitor in Staphylococcus aureus that suppresses endopeptidase activity by presenting a rigid inhibitory surface to metalloproteases. By coordinating zinc to stabilize its inhibitory conformation, it binds and blocks secreted bacterial proteases, thereby restraining proteolysis that would otherwise compromise cellular integrity and modulate extracellular nutrient acquisition.

A calcium- and diacylglycerol-activated serine/threonine kinase that assembles at stimulated membranes via lipid-sensing modules and then phosphorylates diverse cytoplasmic and nuclear substrates to coordinate receptor-driven signaling with transcriptional control, cytoskeletal remodeling, and cell survival. By shuttling between the plasma membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus, it integrates second-messenger and calcium cues to modulate pathways that stabilize proteins, restrain ubiquitin-mediated turnover, and enhance DNA repair capacity.

A nucleo-cytoplasmic ADP-ribosyltransferase that senses DNA damage via N-terminal zinc fingers, assembles repair scaffolds through central regulatory and BRCT modules, and uses a C-terminal catalytic core to build poly(ADP-ribose) chains from NAD+. By modifying chromatin and repair factors, it transiently marks chromatin to recruit and organize repair machinery, thereby driving post-translational modification events that coordinate genome maintenance primarily in the nucleus, with a secondary soluble pool in the cytoplasm.

A lentiviral accessory adaptor that is packaged into the virion and subsequently operates in the cytoplasm and nucleus to assemble host protein complexes essential for replication. By using a non-enzymatic binding scaffold, it recruits nuclear transport and chromatin-associated factors to promote nuclear entry and transcriptional permissiveness, while triggering host cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis. Its assembly role likely couples to host metabolic pathways indirectly, positioning pathways of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis near viral replication hubs. The protein is associated with the viral capsid and functions through multivalent interactions rather than catalysis.

A small membrane-associated assembly factor that organizes late-stage virion assembly and egress in pseudorabies virus. It operates through multivalent binding to recruit and escort viral structural and tegument components from cytoplasmic assembly zones to lysosome-derived membranes, where budding is executed. By scaffolding membrane-proximal complexes and retargeting them to endolysosomal compartments, it coordinates virion assembly and release without intrinsic catalytic activity.

A type I membrane adhesion receptor that forms the extracellular and signaling half of an integrin heterodimer. Its β-propeller head and immunoglobulin-like stalk create a high-avidity binding platform for extracellular ligands and cell-surface counter-receptors, while a short cytoplasmic tail recruits intracellular adaptors to control activation and signaling. Through bidirectional adhesion and signaling, it stabilizes cell–cell and cell–matrix contacts that shape vascular and immune interfaces and contribute to neural plasticity and memory.

A soybean seed storage globulin that assembles a cupin-based oligomer to accumulate and depot-store nitrogen-rich protein during seed development. It is synthesized through the secretory pathway and deposited into extracellular storage pools of maturing seeds, where its stable trimer/hexamer assemblies sequester nutrients and help buffer the embryo during desiccation and germination. Its mechanism relies on a jelly-roll scaffold that drives oligomerization and long-term nutrient reservoir activity.

A soluble human enzyme that hydrolyzes acyl phosphate bonds, thereby dissipating the energy of acyl-phosphate intermediates and stabilizing phosphate balance in the cell. Its single acylphosphatase-like fold forms a catalytic pocket that activates water to cleave phosphorus-containing anhydrides, and it likely functions as a homodimer to maintain active-site geometry. Operating primarily in the cytoplasm, it modulates reactive acyl phosphate species arising during metabolism and signaling, with occasional association with plastid-enriched fractions possible.

A soluble mitotic cyclin that assembles and activates kinase complexes to control late cell-cycle transitions. Its bipartite cyclin-box scaffold binds partner proteins and configures associated kinases that drive G2/M-associated phosphorylation cascades. By organizing these assemblies in the cytoplasm, it modulates pathways that restrain oocyte maturation and fine-tune meiotic/mitotic progression, likely through transient complexes that position and regulate cell-cycle effectors.

A soluble endonuclease that forms the catalytic core of bacterial nucleotide-excision repair. It assembles with damage-recognition and assembly modules to position two metal-dependent nuclease centers that execute the dual incisions flanking a DNA lesion. By orchestrating precise cuts and handing off the processed substrate to downstream repair factors, it operates within intracellular repair assemblies that act on chromosomal DNA in the bacterial interior.

A human small GTPase that cycles between GTP- and GDP-bound states to control cytoskeletal and membrane-associated assemblies central to innate immunity. By switching conformations, it recruits effector proteins that remodel actin and coordinate signaling at the cell periphery, thereby promoting antimicrobial defenses against Gram-negative bacteria. It operates primarily in the cytoplasm with transient engagement of the plasma membrane, where receptor-proximal immune pathways and phagocytic machinery are organized.

A mitochondrial heme-dependent monooxygenase that uses electrons from the mitochondrial ferredoxin system to oxidize cholesterol-derived sterol intermediates, channeling metabolic flux toward steroid hormone production. It operates as a soluble, matrix-facing enzyme within mitochondria, where it receives reducing power via ferredoxin and ferredoxin reductase to activate oxygen at a heme center and perform oxidative transformations that feed the steroidogenic pathway.

A diacylglycerol/phorbol-ester–regulated serine/threonine kinase that cycles between cytosol and membranes to coordinate receptor-driven signaling, cytoskeletal remodeling, and vesicle trafficking. Its N-terminal membrane-targeting modules recruit the enzyme to DAG-enriched sites at the plasma membrane and endoplasmic reticulum, where the C-terminal kinase core phosphorylates substrates that dampen exocytosis and calcium flux. Through these phosphorylation programs it modulates GPCR pathways, restrains dopamine release, and contributes to broader stress-responsive signaling circuits.

A soluble peroxisomal oxidase in fruit fly that converts uric acid to 5-oxouroic acid, initiating the pathway that feeds into allantoin production. Its catalytic center uses oxygen to drive oxidative cleavage of urate, generating hydrogen peroxide that is handled within the peroxisomal matrix. By supplying the key precursor for allantoin biosynthesis and operating in an oxidative compartment, it channels purine-derived nitrogen toward amide-containing end products while coordinating with peroxisomal import and redox systems.

A secreted serine endopeptidase that is synthesized as an autoinhibited zymogen and activated in the secretory pathway to cleave dibasic motifs in proproteins. Its N-terminal inhibitory segment ensures spatiotemporal control, while a subtilisin-like catalytic core executes endoproteolysis and a C-terminal P domain stabilizes calcium-dependent folding and substrate specificity. By processing precursors of secreted and extracellular proteins, it drives maturation of signaling molecules and other cargo in the extracellular milieu.

A nuclear transcriptional regulator that uses an N-terminal repression cassette to assemble corepressor complexes and a C-terminal array of zinc-finger modules to anchor these assemblies at specific genomic sites. By recruiting chromatin-silencing machinery and stabilizing repressive complexes on chromatin, it down-modulates transcriptional output in the nucleus through modular protein–protein interactions and sequence-directed targeting.

A calcium- and diacylglycerol-regulated serine/threonine kinase that cycles between cytoplasm, plasma membrane, and nucleus to coordinate signaling with transcriptional and secretory programs. Lipid- and calcium-sensing modules drive membrane recruitment and nuclear shuttling, enabling phosphorylation of cytoplasmic and nuclear substrates that govern apoptosis, differentiation, and proliferation. By coupling membrane-derived second messengers to gene-expression machinery and endocrine secretion, it integrates acute signaling with sustained transcriptional control.

A lentiviral accessory adaptor that is essential for productive infection. It functions primarily through multivalent protein binding to assemble host protein complexes that dampen apoptosis and stabilize replication-permissive states. Its soluble architecture supports a cytoplasmic pool that captures and redirects host factors, followed by nuclear engagement where it modulates genome surveillance and chromatin-associated assemblies. Together these activities coordinate cytoplasmic and nuclear pathways that safeguard infected cells and promote efficient viral replication.

A lentiviral adaptor that shuttles between the cytoplasm and nucleus of sooty mangabey monkey cells, where it binds host protein complexes to subvert antiviral defenses. By assembling multivalent interactions rather than catalyzing reactions, it redirects nuclear transport and proteostasis pathways to suppress host defenses and promote viral replication. Its nucleocytoplasmic trafficking positions it to engage nuclear pore and import/export machinery in the host nucleus while assembling cytoplasmic complexes that bias ubiquitin–proteasome pathways.

A secreted four-helix bundle cytokine that signals in the extracellular milieu to modulate immune and epithelial pathways. By presenting a conserved receptor-binding surface, it assembles receptor complexes that activate JAK–STAT signaling, thereby tuning cellular programs engaged during cold exposure and other stresses. Its soluble nature and cytokine architecture position it as an extracellular modulator that coordinates tissue and immune responses through receptor-mediated signaling.

A classical, lipid-gated serine/threonine kinase that is activated by diacylglycerol and calcium. It cycles between cytoplasm and nucleus and transiently associates with membranes, where it initiates phosphorylation cascades that regulate transcription and secretory pathways. By coupling membrane-proximal second-messenger sensing to phosphorylation of cytoplasmic and nuclear targets, it coordinates gene-expression programs and contributes to hormone secretion through control of vesicle trafficking and exocytosis.

A nuclear serine/threonine kinase that belongs to the cyclin-dependent kinase clade and functions as a regulated signaling hub for cell cycle control and differentiation. Its CDK-like catalytic core and regulatory features enable phosphorylation of nuclear substrates, particularly transcriptional regulators, thereby dampening DNA-binding activity and shaping gene-expression programs that coordinate proliferation and lineage decisions.

A secreted serine endopeptidase that is synthesized with an autoinhibitory pro-segment, activated in the secretory pathway, and stabilized by a calcium-dependent P domain to cleave precursor proteins at paired basic sites. By executing limited proteolysis outside the cell, it activates and matures secreted and membrane-associated substrates, thereby driving extracellular protein processing and maturation.

A soluble cytosolic oxygenase that uses a cupin β-barrel to coordinate a ferrous cofactor and activate molecular oxygen for the oxidative conversion of cysteine to 3‑oxo‑L‑cysteine. This reaction initiates cysteine breakdown and supports downstream pathways that maintain sulfur amino acid and glutathione homeostasis. The jelly‑roll scaffold stabilizes the catalytic iron center and likely hosts a structural zinc site, enabling efficient dioxygenation within the cytoplasm.

A secreted lipocalin that binds diverse retinoids and fatty-acid–like ligands and likely fine-tunes their pools by high-affinity sequestration and a modest intrinsic isomerization activity. After entering the secretory pathway and transiting the endoplasmic reticulum, it accumulates outside the cell where it buffers and redistributes retinoids. By stabilizing retinoid intermediates and shaping their availability, it supports downstream isoprenoid-related pathways and coordinates extracellular retinoid exchange with cellular uptake routes.

A soluble mitochondrial site-specific endonuclease in fission yeast that uses a LAGLIDADG catalytic core to cleave DNA and drive intron mobility within mitochondrial nucleoids. By creating precise double-strand breaks that are repaired to incorporate mobile genetic elements, it coordinates with mitochondrial RNA-processing assemblies to align DNA transactions with RNA splicing pathways. Its multivalent protein-binding surfaces likely stabilize assemblies with RNA–DNA complexes in the mitochondrial matrix.

An endoplasmic reticulum–anchored, single-pass membrane glycosyltransferase that catalyzes glucuronic acid transfer onto diverse hydrophobic molecules, thereby neutralizing and facilitating the clearance or further processing of endogenous and xenobiotic substrates. Its luminal catalytic core installs glucuronyl groups on steroids, bile acid–related intermediates, and vitamin D metabolites, integrating with ER-centered detoxification pathways and broader metabolic networks. The membrane anchor secures ER residency and coordinates with luminal assembly and transport systems that supply the glucuronyl donor and route conjugated products.

A cytosolic thiamine diphosphate-dependent enzyme that forms a soluble dimer to transfer two-carbon ketol groups between sugar phosphates. By stabilizing a divalent-cation-activated cofactor and executing carbanion chemistry, it interconverts sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, erythrose-4-phosphate, and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, thereby sustaining the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway and balancing nucleotide precursor and redox cofactor production in yeast.

A human cytoskeletal GTPase that serves as the nucleation-competent core of microtubule-organizing assemblies. It concentrates at centrosomes and other organizing centers, where it binds partner proteins to form nucleation templates that initiate minus-end formation without itself polymerizing. Its N-terminal nucleotide-binding engine and C-terminal interaction platform cooperate to stabilize ring-like nucleation assemblies, thereby seeding α/β-tubulin growth and shaping the architecture of the microtubule network.

A soluble human rotamase that accelerates the rate-limiting cis–trans isomerization of proline peptide bonds, thereby promoting efficient folding and conformational switching of client proteins. Its cyclophilin catalytic core operates in the cytoplasm but is likely recruited to membrane-bounded compartments where folding and assembly pathways concentrate. By transiently associating with organelle surfaces, it fine-tunes maturation and assembly of membrane-associated complexes through chaperone-coupled isomerization chemistry.

A nuclear cyclin-fold scaffold that assembles and activates nuclear regulatory complexes. By using its bipartite cyclin architecture, it recruits and tunes partner enzymes to coordinate transcriptional control and ubiquitin-dependent pathways in the nucleus. This assembly role enables ubiquitin ligase activity within associated complexes, reshapes host cellular programs, and indirectly modulates small GTPase circuits by adjusting gene expression and the turnover of GTPase regulators.

A lentiviral accessory adaptor that is packaged in the virion and shuttles between the host cytoplasm and nucleus. It binds nucleic acids and chromatin to assemble host complexes that bias cellular pathways toward viral fitness. By engaging DNA and coordinating with RNA-processing machinery, it organizes host assemblies that support replication and assembly, consistent with a nucleic acid–binding scaffold that operates downstream of entry and within nuclear compartments.

A virion-packaged lentiviral adaptor that associates with the particle interior and uses multivalent protein binding to assemble regulatory complexes that bias host pathways toward replication. By coupling to the capsid and core matrix, it is delivered into the incoming particle and then orchestrates host complex assembly that tunes nuclear transport and immune signaling. This adaptor-driven modulation dampens specific signaling systems and supports early post-entry remodeling, consistent with a role in the virion and viral capsid.

A soluble luminal serine endopeptidase that is synthesized with an autoinhibitory prodomain, trafficked through the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi, and activated in acidic secretory compartments to cleave paired-basic motifs in prohormones and proproteins. Its calcium-stabilized auxiliary domain tunes activity and specificity, enabling maturation of peptide precursors within secretory granules and the extracellular milieu. By coupling intramolecular activation with precise endoproteolysis, it drives zymogen activation and broader protein processing along the secretory pathway.

A cytoplasmic adaptor that uses two phosphotyrosine-recognition modules to assemble signaling complexes. Its N-terminal module captures NPXY-containing and phosphorylated receptor tails, while the C-terminal module stabilizes phosphotyrosine-rich assemblies, together enabling multivalent protein binding that routes signals through intracellular pathways. By scaffolding receptor-proximal complexes in the cytoplasm, it modulates the strength and timing of downstream cascades.

A small ubiquitin-like modifier in mouse that operates as a soluble cytoplasmic conjugate, forming transient thioester intermediates and becoming covalently attached to lysine residues on target proteins to regulate their activity. By driving a dedicated neddylation pathway, it activates cullin-based ubiquitin ligase assemblies and broadly tunes proteostasis and cell-cycle–linked signaling through reversible protein modification.

A nuclear, ligand-responsive transcriptional regulator that uses an N‑terminal DNA-binding module and a tandem PAS system to sense small molecules and assemble heterodimeric complexes that activate RNA polymerase II–dependent transcription. By coupling environmental and metabolic cues to gene expression, it drives programs associated with xenobiotic and organic cyclic compound responses and enhances transcriptional output from target promoters through regulated dimerization and coactivator recruitment.

A soluble human flavin-dependent monooxygenase that uses a tightly bound flavin cofactor and NADPH to activate molecular oxygen and insert a single oxygen atom into diverse nitrogen- and sulfur-containing small molecules. Operating in the cytoplasm and functionally adjacent to intracellular organelles, it supports broad heteroatom-oxygenation chemistry that contributes to cellular metabolism and detoxification. Its mechanism proceeds through a C4a-hydroperoxyflavin intermediate formed and resolved within a Rossmann-like dinucleotide-binding core characteristic of FAD/NADPH-utilizing enzymes.

A soluble adaptor that forms dimers to clamp phosphorylated client proteins and remodel their conformations and interactions. By selectively binding short phospho-motifs, it stabilizes and organizes kinase-centered signaling assemblies, thereby tuning pathway flux and promoting kinase activation. Its soluble nature supports shuttling between cytoplasm and nucleus, where it coordinates phosphorylation-dependent signaling and transcriptional control through multivalent scaffolding.

A soluble human non-heme iron oxygenase that assembles a vicinal oxygen chelate fold into a homodimeric enzyme catalyzing dioxygenation of aromatic keto-acids along the tyrosine degradation route. It binds Fe(II) to activate molecular oxygen and convert 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate within tyrosine catabolism, with ancillary activity toward 2-hydroxyglutarate. The enzyme operates primarily in the cytoplasm and can access the nucleus, where iron–oxygen chemistry and metabolic signaling intersect. Dimerization stabilizes the active site and coordinates with cellular iron and redox systems to sustain pathway flux.

A soluble, iron-dependent dioxygenase in rat that assembles as a homodimer and uses a vicinal oxygen chelate fold to bind Fe(II), activate molecular oxygen, and catalyze a key step in tyrosine breakdown. By converting 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate along the tyrosine catabolic route, it helps balance intracellular pools of tyrosine-derived metabolites that intersect with stress-response and xenobiotic pathways. The enzyme predominantly operates in the cytoplasm, with a secondary nuclear pool likely reflecting soluble, regulatory behavior that couples metabolic state to nuclear processes.

A multi-pass inner-membrane channel subunit in baker’s yeast that forms the core of the mitochondrial presequence translocase. It assembles and stabilizes a translocation pore that accepts transit peptide–bearing precursors arriving from the outer membrane system and couples their passage across the inner membrane to an ATP-driven import motor on the matrix side. By coordinating partner binding and membrane-embedded architecture, it enables efficient delivery of precursor proteins into the mitochondrial matrix.

A meiosis-specialized adaptor that organizes early recombination assemblies in budding yeast. It operates as a soluble scaffold that binds other proteins to drive meiotic progression while being dispensable for mitosis. By assembling recombination complexes in the nucleus and promoting their regulated release, it likely couples chromatin-associated assembly to nuclear export pathways, ensuring timely redistribution of factors required for crossover formation and meiotic timing.

A soluble ATP-driven helicase that binds and remodels ribonucleoprotein assemblies in baker’s yeast. Its N-terminal regulatory module and central ATPase core power strand/RNP remodeling, while a C-terminal Upf1-like region stabilizes nucleic acid engagement. Operating in both cytoplasm and nucleus, it likely coordinates RNA surveillance and assembly pathways that connect nuclear RNP maturation to mitochondrial biogenesis, thereby contributing to assembly of respiratory complex I and transiently associating with the telomerase machinery.

A nuclear scaffold subunit of the TFIIH complex that organizes transcription and DNA repair machinery. Its N-terminal scaffold core and C-terminal zinc-finger/C1-like module create a multivalent platform that assembles and stabilizes TFIIH components, positioning helicase and accessory modules to open DNA during lesion processing and to support promoter clearance during RNA polymerase II transcription. By coordinating partner binding and complex integrity, it couples nucleotide excision repair with transcriptional control in the nucleus.

A secreted human cytokine that adopts a four-helix bundle to bind cell-surface receptor complexes and trigger signaling that tempers immune cytotoxicity and supports endothelial survival. By engaging its cognate receptor system in the extracellular space, it initiates pathways that dampen complement-driven cell damage and reduce apoptosis in endothelial cells, consistent with a soluble mediator that operates through receptor-mediated signaling rather than enzymatic activity.

A soluble cytoplasmic enzyme that hydrolyzes acyl–phosphate bonds and also cleaves carbamoyl phosphate, thereby quenching reactive phosphorylated intermediates and maintaining phosphate balance in central metabolism. Its conserved catalytic pocket forms a transient phosphoenzyme intermediate that directs water attack on acyl–phosphate substrates, preventing accumulation of potentially damaging species and stabilizing cytosolic energy and nucleotide pathways.

A phycobiliprotein that assembles into antenna complexes of cyanobacteria, using a globin-like scaffold to bind linear tetrapyrrole chromophores and organize energy-transfer pathways. By stabilizing higher-order assemblies that feed excitation energy into photosynthetic and associated anabolic routes, it supports diverse biosyntheses, including pathways that generate biotin. The protein operates as a soluble, peripherally membrane-associated component of large complexes, with assembly surfaces that can also engage nucleic acids.

A ligand-activated bHLH-PAS transcriptional regulator that senses small aromatic and other xenobiotic-like cues in the cytoplasm, translocates to the nucleus upon activation, and assembles into transcriptional regulator complexes to stimulate RNA polymerase II-driven gene expression. Its basic helix-loop-helix region confers sequence-specific DNA recognition and core promoter engagement, while tandem PAS domains and a C-terminal PAC motif govern ligand responsiveness and heterodimer formation. By coupling environmental and metabolic signals to promoter-proximal control, it coordinates transcriptional programs that respond to xenobiotics and organic cyclic compounds.

A multi-pass membrane transporter at the cell surface that uses a major facilitator architecture to drive proton-coupled transmembrane movement of small hydrophobic hormones and metabolites. By alternating access across the membrane, it mediates bidirectional transport of thyroid hormones and likely retinoids and related monocarboxylates, thereby tuning intracellular hormone pools that feed into thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion pathways. Its plasma-membrane residency and secondary-active mechanism position it as a key regulator of endocrine and metabolic fluxes at the cell periphery.

A soluble adenylate-forming ligase in E. coli that activates 2-succinylbenzoate to its CoA thioester through an ATP-dependent two-step mechanism, supplying a key activated intermediate for menaquinone biosynthesis. The enzyme operates as a cytosolic assembly that likely forms homotypic complexes, using an AMP-binding core to generate the adenylate and a C-terminal clamp to drive thioesterification with CoA, thereby sustaining the quinone-producing branch of central metabolism.

A cytosolic ATP-driven DNA repair factor that forms the core of the excision machinery. It uses a helicase-like ATPase engine to load onto distorted DNA, assemble with partner repair proteins, and stabilize lesion sites so that endonucleases can incise damaged strands. By orchestrating lesion recognition and handoff within a soluble repair assembly, it promotes excision-based genome maintenance and interfaces with broader pathways that resolve double-strand breaks.

A soluble beta-propeller scaffold that shuttles between the cytoplasm and peroxisomes to mediate PTS2-dependent cargo delivery into the peroxisomal matrix. By using a WD40 repeat architecture to bind PTS2-bearing proteins and assemble transient import complexes, it coordinates cargo capture and handoff to peroxisomal import machinery. This activity sustains peroxisomal enzyme composition and thereby supports ether lipid biosynthesis in baker’s yeast.

A multi-pass inner-membrane translocase subunit in baker’s yeast that organizes the presequence-dependent import pathway across the mitochondrial inner membrane. By forming a binding-driven scaffold and gating module for the translocation channel, it coordinates assembly and regulation of the inner-membrane translocase, enabling efficient transfer of precursor proteins into and across the membrane in concert with matrix-side import motors.

A soluble sugar-phosphate phosphatase in baker’s yeast that uses a metal-dependent catalytic core to hydrolyze phosphomonoesters, thereby tuning pools of phosphorylated carbohydrates and indirectly sustaining glycerol production during osmoadaptation. Its activity supports broader carbohydrate metabolism and stress resilience, with a primary expectation of cytosolic function and a plausible secreted/pericellular role via non-classical export that allows scavenging of extracellular sugar phosphates and modulation of extracellular phosphate balance.

A signal-activated transcriptional regulator that shuttles between cytoplasm and nucleus to couple cytokine and growth factor inputs to gene expression programs controlling proliferation and differentiation. It assembles via N-terminal and coiled-coil modules, binds DNA through a central recognition core, and uses a C-terminal phosphotyrosine-recognition unit to dimerize and become transcriptionally active after receptor-proximal phosphorylation. This architecture enables stimulus-dependent nuclear entry and activation of target genes downstream of pathways such as leukemia inhibitory factor signaling, with transient association to membrane-proximal receptor complexes preceding nuclear transcriptional control.

A soluble lipocalin that folds into a β-barrel cavity to bind retinoids and other hydrophobic lipids, thereby shaping extracellular and secretory-pathway pools of lipid mediators. By stabilizing and subtly isomerizing lipidic substrates within its barrel, it modulates pathways that generate arachidonate-derived products and prostaglandins while buffering retinoid availability. It traffics through the endoplasmic reticulum en route to secretion and operates primarily in the extracellular milieu, where it chaperones and fine-tunes lipid signaling chemistry.

A cytoplasmic lipid-metabolizing enzyme that combines phospholipase and acyltransferase chemistries to regulate neutral lipid and phospholipid pathways. It hydrolyzes ester bonds in triacylglycerols and phospholipids to generate fatty acids and diacylglycerol, while also catalyzing acyl transfer that can rebalance acyl flux. Through this dual hydrolase/transferase mechanism, it contributes to intracellular lipid handling and energy balance within the cytoplasm, likely operating near lipid droplets and transient membrane interfaces.

A soluble yeast phosphatase that hydrolyzes sugar phosphates to drive glycerol production and osmoadaptation. It operates in the cytoplasm using a metal-dependent catalytic core to dephosphorylate glycerol-3-phosphate and related intermediates, thereby relieving phosphate inhibition and channeling carbon toward glycerol accumulation during osmotic stress. While its primary activity is cytoplasmic, a minor fraction may appear outside the cell under stress conditions. The enzyme functions as a metabolic valve that sustains glycerol biosynthesis and broader carbohydrate flux.

A nuclear, ligand-activated bHLH-PAS transcriptional regulator that senses small hydrophobic cues to control gene expression. Its N-terminal basic helix-loop-helix module binds DNA, while tandem PAS domains and a C-terminal PAC motif assemble a ligand-gated heterodimer that recruits transcriptional machinery. By coupling environmental and metabolic signals to promoter occupancy, it drives transcriptional programs that elevate responses to xenobiotics and organic cyclic compounds and broadly enhance transcription in the nucleus.

A secreted cytokine that adopts a four-helix bundle to act as an extracellular ligand, engaging a class I cytokine receptor complex to trigger JAK–STAT signaling. Through this pathway it promotes epithelial cell proliferation and suppresses apoptosis, while coordinating immune responses and tissue repair characteristic of IL-13-type cytokines.

A signal-activated transcriptional regulator that shuttles between cytoplasm and nucleus. It remains cytoplasmic in a latent state and, upon tyrosine phosphorylation downstream of cytokine and growth-factor pathways, dimerizes through a phosphotyrosine-recognition module and accumulates in the nucleus. There it binds specific promoter elements and recruits co-regulators to drive gene expression programs that implement responses to cytokines such as leukemia inhibitory factor.

A type I membrane adhesion receptor that forms a heterodimer with a beta integrin to bind extracellular matrix ligands such as fibronectin and fibrinogen via a divalent cation–dependent propeller headpiece. Its ectodomain and immunoglobulin-like stalk transmit conformational signals across the membrane to a short cytoplasmic tail that recruits intracellular effectors. Through this adhesion–signaling axis, it anchors cells to matrix and initiates integrin-mediated pathways that coordinate cell adhesion and broader signaling at the plasma membrane.

A soluble sugar-phosphate transferase that uses a thiamine diphosphate–dependent mechanism to move two-carbon units between ketose and aldose phosphates, thereby sustaining the non-oxidative arm of the pentose phosphate pathway in Haemophilus influenzae. Its bilobal cofactor-binding core and conserved active-site motifs generate a thiamine ylide and require divalent cations for catalysis. Operating as a cytosolic oligomer, it balances ribose-5-phosphate supply and central carbon flux by coupling pentose phosphate chemistry to neighboring pathways.

A soluble cytoplasmic amidohydrolase that assembles as a homodimer and uses a divalent-metal catalytic center to hydrolyze the amide bond of acetyl-diaminopimelate, producing lysine and acetyl-CoA. By executing this committed step in the diaminopimelate route to lysine, it feeds both amino acid biosynthesis and cell-envelope precursor pathways. The dimerization core organizes the active site and stabilizes metal coordination, while zinc or cobalt binding tunes catalysis. Its soluble architecture and pathway context place it in the cytoplasm, where it likely forms transient assemblies with neighboring enzymes to streamline lysine production and downstream envelope biogenesis.

A soluble ThDP-dependent carbon-transfer enzyme that catalyzes reversible two‑carbon exchanges between sugar phosphates, thereby sustaining the non‑oxidative branch of the pentose‑phosphate pathway and balancing ribose‑5‑phosphate and glycolytic intermediates. It operates primarily in the cytosol as a likely homodimeric assembly that binds thiamine diphosphate to form a covalent intermediate and channel carbon flux. During host-associated growth, transient association with vacuolar and extracellular vesicle systems may position the enzyme within vacuolar compartments and extracellular membrane-bounded organelles, reflecting its central role in metabolic networks that underpin energy and precursor supply.

A human transcriptional co-regulator that shuttles between cytoplasm and nucleus to coordinate gene expression programs controlling cell cycle progression, differentiation, and motility. It binds TEAD-class transcription factors through a conserved docking element and uses tandem WW modules to assemble PY-motif-containing partners, thereby coupling transcriptional regulation with cytoskeletal and trafficking pathways. By organizing these assemblies, it modulates where client proteins reside within the cell and tunes epithelial–mesenchymal and proliferative outputs through context-dependent nuclear activity and cytoplasmic scaffolding.

A modular transcriptional co-regulator that shuttles between cytoplasm and nucleus to coordinate gene expression with cytoskeletal remodeling. It uses a TEAD-docking element to engage transcription factor complexes and tandem WW modules to bind PPxY-containing partners, thereby assembling regulatory hubs that influence epithelial–mesenchymal programs and cell morphology. By coupling transcriptional control to adhesion and actin–myosin pathways, it modulates cell shape and cytoskeleton organization through dynamic nucleocytoplasmic trafficking.

A cytoplasmic, cortex-enriched non-receptor tyrosine kinase that uses tandem phosphotyrosine-recognition modules to dock onto activated receptor assemblies and then employs a high-fidelity catalytic core to phosphorylate downstream substrates. By assembling at receptor-proximal clusters, it drives MAPK pathway activation and broader intracellular signaling. Its SH2-driven recruitment to immune and adhesion receptor complexes positions it at the cell cortex and cytoplasm, where it orchestrates phosphorylation cascades that can be co-opted by symbiotic or parasitic effectors to modulate host signal transduction.

A nuclear serine/threonine kinase in fruit fly that binds ATP and phosphorylates chromatin-associated substrates to modulate transcription and growth programs. By acting on histones and nuclear regulators, it elevates biosynthetic capacity and delays mitotic entry, thereby promoting cell growth and increased cell size. Its activity is tuned by cyclin-like regulation and executed through a bilobal kinase core that aligns ATP and substrate for efficient phosphotransfer within the nucleus.

A secreted extracellular matrix-associated protein in mouse that uses a large protease-like scaffold to bind retinol and organize matrix-associated remodeling. By anchoring within collagen-rich extracellular matrices, it stabilizes and presents hydrophobic retinoids while coordinating extracellular proteolysis and matrix turnover. This dual ligand- and matrix-handling role positions it as a retinoid-handling hub at the tissue surface, where it modulates retinoid availability and extracellular processing.

A single-pass type II membrane receptor in mouse that displays an extracellular C-type lectin-like domain to capture glycosylated ligands and drive endocytic uptake at the cell surface. By coupling extracellular binding to internalization and downstream signaling, it modulates cargo trafficking and matrix/growth-factor availability, thereby influencing pathways that contribute to skeletal system development. Its mechanism centers on Ca2+-stabilized ligand recognition by the lectin-like domain and assembly of endocytic machinery through its cytosolic tail.

A nucleocytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase that operates under cyclin/cofactor control to coordinate transcriptional regulation with autophagy. It concentrates in the nucleus to phosphorylate transcriptional substrates, including the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II, thereby tuning gene expression and RNA processing. In the cytoplasm, it promotes autophagic flux and integrates host–virus interface decisions that influence programmed cell death. By shuttling between compartments and assembling with regulatory partners, it functions as a timing hub that links transcriptional checkpoints to autophagy and antiviral pathways.

A soluble short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase that uses a nicotinamide-dependent redox center to reversibly interconvert ketone and hydroxyl groups on steroids, bile acids, and retinoids. Operating predominantly in the cytosol and at the endoplasmic reticulum interface, it fine-tunes corticosteroid and bile acid pools and likely contributes to broader lipid-derived signaling pathways. Its catalytic mechanism relies on a conserved Tyr–Lys active-site motif and a Rossmann-like cofactor-binding fold that together mediate hydride transfer during steroid dehydrogenation.

A soluble short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase that uses a nicotinamide-dependent catalytic core to interconvert hydroxysteroids and ketosteroids central to glucocorticoid and androgen pathways. By binding NAD(H)/NADP(H) and aligning steroid substrates for hydride transfer, it modulates the levels of 20‑alpha‑ketosteroids and 17‑beta‑hydroxysteroids, thereby shaping alcohol/ketone fluxes within steroid metabolism. Its activity integrates into endoplasmic reticulum–proximal assemblies that manage steroid processing and conjugation.

A soluble cytoplasmic exoribonuclease that degrades single-stranded RNA processively from the 3′ end. Its N-terminal catalytic engine performs phosphate-dependent nucleotide removal, while a C-terminal KH–S1 RNA-binding tail captures and threads RNA into the active channel. By turning over tRNA, rRNA, and mRNA intermediates, it drives RNA quality control and turnover in the bacterial cytoplasm and assembles into ribonuclease hubs that fine-tune RNA decay pathways.

A cytoplasmic phosphoinositide-cleaving enzyme that assembles a membrane-targeted catalytic core to hydrolyze phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate. Its N-terminal lipid-binding module and calcium-sensing elements recruit and activate the enzyme at membrane surfaces, where a bipartite catalytic center performs phosphodiester cleavage. The C-terminal regulatory tail couples activity to heterotrimeric G-protein pathways, positioning the enzyme as a central node in second-messenger signaling that links receptor inputs to calcium and protein kinase C pathways within the cytoplasm.

A soluble short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase that uses a nicotinamide-dependent catalytic center to interconvert alcohol and ketone groups on hydrophobic substrates. It stereospecifically reduces isoeugenol to eugenol and oxidizes diverse carbonyl-bearing molecules, while efficiently processing 3α-hydroxysteroids and diterpenoid pathway intermediates. By tuning the stereochemistry of labdane-related intermediates and steroid-like substrates, it supports diterpenoid biosynthesis and operates near endoplasmic reticulum membranes where hydrophobic intermediates and partner enzymes concentrate.

A soluble mitochondrial matrix oxidoreductase that couples a molybdenum-cofactor catalytic center with a cytochrome b5-like heme module to oxidize sulfur-containing substrates and relay electrons within the organelle. By binding molybdopterin and heme and operating as a dimeric soluble scaffold, it transfers electrons from thiol/disulfide chemistry into mitochondrial respiration, thereby supporting carbon utilization and tuning metabolism to nutrient availability in the matrix environment.

A soluble short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase that uses a nicotinamide-dependent catalytic center to interconvert hydroxysteroids and ketosteroids central to bile acid and glucocorticoid pathways. Operating at the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum, it binds NAD(H)/NADP(H) and employs a conserved Tyr–Lys catalytic system to transfer hydride efficiently to lipophilic steroid and bile acid intermediates, thereby shaping the balance of steroid and bile acid metabolism.

A soluble bacterial termination factor that uses an RNA-binding OB-fold to capture nascent transcripts and a C-terminal ATP-driven motor to translocate along single-stranded RNA, thereby destabilizing RNA–DNA hybrids and releasing elongating transcription complexes. It assembles with the transcription machinery through dedicated N-terminal and ATPase modules, acting as a rho-dependent termination machine that operates independently of intrinsic termination signals and functions at the nucleoid–cytoplasm interface in Streptomyces lividans.

A nuclear transcriptional regulator that uses a KRAB repression module and a multi–C2H2 zinc-finger array to bind specific genomic sites and assemble corepressor complexes that silence target genes. By stabilizing homotypic assemblies on chromatin and recruiting canonical repression machinery, it modulates developmental transcriptional programs that shape branching morphogenesis and related differentiation pathways.

A Golgi-localized bifunctional enzyme that executes two sequential steps in heparan sulfate maturation: it first removes acetyl groups from glucosamine residues and then transfers sulfate to the newly exposed amines. By coupling deacetylation and sulfation within one polypeptide, it streamlines and patterns glycosaminoglycan assembly, shaping the sulfation code that underpins heparan sulfate proteoglycan biosynthesis and downstream signaling functions.

A soluble ureohydrolase in Bacillus caldovelox that hydrolyzes the guanidinium group of arginine to produce ornithine and urea, thereby routing nitrogen and carbon through arginine metabolism. Its fold organizes a binuclear manganese center that activates water for catalysis and explains robustness under fluctuating metal availability. The enzyme likely operates primarily in the cytosol to integrate with nitrogen assimilation and ornithine pathways, with a minor extracellular fraction possible via nonclassical release.

A soluble quorum-sensing transcriptional activator in Yersinia that uses an N-terminal signal-sensing module to homodimerize and a C-terminal winged-helix effector to bind promoter DNA and stimulate transcription of virulence regulons. By coupling small-molecule signal detection to assembly on target promoters, it elevates expression of invasion and cytotoxicity pathways that remodel host cell biology. The protein operates in the cytoplasm and becomes promoter-bound within nucleoprotein assemblies when activated.

A single-pass cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinase that binds membrane-tethered ephrins through a modular extracellular region and signals via an intracellular kinase and SAM scaffold. Ligand-induced clustering activates kinase autophosphorylation and adaptor recruitment, driving cytoskeletal and adhesion remodeling that govern endothelial and lymphatic morphogenesis, epithelial tissue shaping, and directed cell migration. Its membrane-anchored architecture and clustering propensity position it at the plasma membrane where it orchestrates ephrin-dependent signaling assemblies.

A cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinase that binds membrane-tethered ephrin ligands across cell–cell contacts, clusters into higher-order assemblies, and activates an intracellular kinase module to autophosphorylate and signal. This signaling remodels adhesion and cytoskeletal systems to guide endothelial and lymphatic vessel patterning, venous specification, and directed cell migration during morphogenesis. A C-terminal sterile alpha motif stabilizes oligomeric signaling platforms that tune pathway strength and duration at the plasma membrane.

A membrane-proximal adaptor subunit of heterotrimeric G proteins that forms a tight dimer with the beta subunit to stabilize the trimer and tune receptor-driven signaling at the cell surface. By anchoring and organizing the signaling assembly at the plasma membrane, it promotes efficient coupling from activated receptors to downstream effectors and thereby sustains canonical GPCR signal transduction cycles.

A soluble cytoplasmic oxygenase that uses a cupin/jelly-roll scaffold to coordinate a ferrous iron center and activate molecular oxygen for the oxidative breakdown of cysteine. By inserting both oxygen atoms during cysteine oxidation, it generates a reactive sulfenic intermediate that is resolved within the active site, thereby driving cysteine catabolism and sustaining sulfur amino acid homeostasis. The enzyme’s metal-coordinating barrel explains its iron dependence and ancillary zinc interaction, and its cytosolic location positions it to engage redox buffering systems and metabolic partners that manage reactive intermediates.

A membrane-proximal small GTPase switch in mouse that cycles between GTP- and GDP-bound states to control actin remodeling and membrane trafficking. By assembling effector complexes at the cell surface, it drives cell migration and endocytic pathways that feed into innate immune defenses, particularly those that internalize and neutralize Gram-negative bacteria. Its activity is tuned by exchange and hydrolysis cycles that localize signaling to the plasma membrane and coordinate cytoskeletal and vesicular machinery.

A membrane-proximal small GTPase switch that cycles between GTP- and GDP-bound states to control actin remodeling and membrane trafficking. By recruiting effectors that stimulate cytoskeletal assembly and vesicle dynamics, it drives cell motility and coordinates endocytic and autophagic pathways that underpin innate immune and antibacterial defenses. Its action concentrates at the plasma membrane, where it organizes actin-based protrusion and pathogen-uptake machinery.

A nucleo-cytoplasmic adaptor that forms the core of an elongation- and ubiquitin-ligase–linked assembly. Its ubiquitin-like fold creates a high-affinity scaffold that stabilizes the elongin complex and couples it to cullin-based ubiquitin ligases. By organizing and assembling multiprotein complexes, it supports RNA polymerase II–dependent transcription, bridging initiation-proximal events with efficient elongation. The protein functions through multivalent binding rather than catalysis, concentrating in the nucleus for transcriptional control while also assembling and trafficking in the cytoplasm.

A cytoplasmic WD40 β-propeller scaffold that forms the core of heterotrimeric G-protein assemblies. By tightly binding the γ subunit and docking the α subunit and downstream effectors, it stabilizes the inactive complex, promotes nucleotide exchange upon receptor activation, and organizes signaling modules that drive cyclic AMP production and broader GPCR pathways. Its scaffolded assemblies operate at membrane-proximal sites in neurons and photoreceptors, supporting dopamine receptor and prostaglandin-responsive signaling from cytoplasmic pools that dynamically associate with the inner face of the plasma membrane and the photoreceptor outer segment.

A soluble serine/threonine kinase of the ERK class that transduces extracellular cues through a mitogen-activated signaling cascade to regulate gene expression and cytoskeletal dynamics. It cycles between cytoplasm and nucleus, where it phosphorylates transcriptional and structural targets to coordinate developmental programs. By integrating upstream activation with precise substrate docking, it modulates morphogenetic pathways that shape tissue architecture and contributes to morphogenetic events such as dorsal appendage formation in mouse development.

A nucleocytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase that functions as an ERK-class mitogen-activated protein kinase. It binds ATP and, upon activation by upstream kinases, phosphorylates transcriptional regulators and cytoskeletal effectors to transmit mitogenic and stress signals. By shuttling from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, it coordinates gene-expression programs and structural remodeling that together drive morphogenetic processes, including those required for dorsal appendage formation in rat development.

A soluble serine endopeptidase that is synthesized as a latent zymogen and activated in the secretory pathway to cleave proproteins at paired basic residues. It operates within the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus and traffics to secretory granules before release, where it completes hormone and growth factor maturation. Autocatalytic removal of its inhibitory pro-segment enables a subtilisin-like catalytic core stabilized by a calcium-binding P-domain, producing mature bioactive peptides that regulate intercellular signaling.

A calcium- and diacylglycerol-activated serine/threonine kinase that cycles between cytoplasm and membrane surfaces to phosphorylate diverse substrates. Its N-terminal lipid-sensing modules recruit the enzyme to DAG-rich membranes, where calcium-dependent membrane binding aligns the catalytic core for efficient signaling. Through phosphorylation cascades, it modulates transcriptional and cytoskeletal pathways, stabilizes key regulatory proteins by limiting their ubiquitination and proteolysis, and enhances DNA repair responses. The enzyme’s activity integrates membrane-proximal cues with broad control of phosphorylation-dependent networks at the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane and within the cytoplasm.

A calcium- and diacylglycerol-gated serine/threonine kinase that transduces membrane-proximal signals into broad phosphorylation programs. By docking to membranes through lipid- and calcium-sensing modules, it becomes activated and modifies numerous substrates that govern apoptosis, cytoskeletal remodeling, and transcriptional control. Its activity stabilizes selected proteins and dampens ubiquitin- and proteasome-linked pathways, while enhancing DNA repair responses. The enzyme operates primarily at the plasma membrane but dynamically engages cytoplasmic and nuclear targets through regulated membrane association and scaffolded signaling assemblies.

A divisome-associated glycoside hydrolase in E. coli that concentrates at the cell envelope to remodel extracellular glycans during division. Its catalytic core hydrolyzes O-glycosyl bonds, enabling localized degradation of cell-wall-associated polysaccharides that accompanies septation and envelope maintenance. By positioning its activity at division sites, it coordinates with cell-division machinery to fine-tune cell-wall turnover and structural maturation at the envelope interface.

A classical, DAG- and membrane-recruited serine/threonine kinase that cycles between the cytosol and the plasma membrane. Lipid and calcium sensing at its N-terminal modules drives membrane translocation, where the catalytic core phosphorylates targets to propagate intracellular signaling. By coupling DAG/phorbol-ester recognition with Ca2+-tunable membrane docking, it amplifies phosphorylation cascades that regulate cytoskeletal remodeling and vesicle trafficking, thereby coordinating signal transduction and innate immune pathways.

A calcium- and diacylglycerol-gated serine/threonine kinase that cycles between the cytosol and membranes to propagate receptor-driven signals. Its N-terminal lipid-sensing modules recruit it to diacylglycerol-rich sites and coordinate with calcium-dependent membrane binding, which together activate a conserved kinase core and its AGC regulatory tail. By phosphorylating diverse substrates, it drives signal transduction and protein modification cascades that extend from receptor-proximal events to cytosolic responses, including pathways engaged by innate immune receptors.

A soluble human oxidoreductase that uses a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase catalytic core to interconvert hydroxysteroids and ketosteroids.
