By binding nicotinamide cofactors and executing Tyr–Lys-mediated hydride transfer, it processes multiple positions on androstane and pregnane substrates and thereby shapes pathways that include bile acid and steroid hormone metabolism. Its activity supports broader lipid and alcohol metabolic networks and is expected to operate near endoplasmic reticulum interfaces where steroid and xenobiotic processing converge.

A cytoplasmic, centrosome-enriched tubulin-class GTPase that serves as the nucleation core of microtubule-organizing assemblies. By using a regulated GTPase engine coupled to a multivalent interaction platform, it scaffolds ring-shaped nucleation complexes that template minus-end formation, thereby initiating and promoting microtubule assembly within the cytoskeleton and at organizing centers.

A nuclear adaptor that forms the core of an elongation-competent complex and a ubiquitin-ligase scaffold. It uses a SKP1/POZ interaction module to assemble and stabilize a dimeric hub that supports RNA polymerase II elongation and also nucleates Cul2-based ubiquitin ligase assemblies. By organizing partner proteins through multivalent binding surfaces, it sustains transcript elongation in the nucleus and couples this activity to broader protein homeostasis pathways.

A single-pass membrane sensor that resides primarily in the endoplasmic reticulum and couples luminal calcium sensing to store-operated calcium entry. Its N-terminal calcium-binding module detects ER calcium depletion, triggering a conformational switch and oligomerization that exposes a cytosolic activating region. This region engages and potentiates calcium influx pathways at ER–plasma membrane junctions, thereby regulating calcium channel complexes and driving calcium transport and signaling.

A nuclear largest-subunit scaffold of a multisubunit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that builds and gates the active center for RNA synthesis. Its clamp and funnel architectures secure and channel nucleic acids and ribonucleoside triphosphates, enabling highly processive transcription of mRNA precursors and noncoding RNAs. By organizing initiation and elongation interfaces, it assembles with other polymerase components and nuclear cofactors to drive polymerase II–mediated transcription within the nucleus.

A cytoplasmic adaptor that organizes intracellular signaling downstream of receptor and cytokine pathways. It uses tandem phosphotyrosine-recognition modules to clamp onto phosphorylated receptor and adaptor motifs, assembling signalosomes that route inputs from cell-surface receptors into downstream cascades controlling growth and differentiation. By stabilizing and positioning enzymatic partners rather than catalyzing reactions itself, it modulates the amplitude and timing of intracellular signal transduction.

A single-pass cell-surface receptor that recognizes and internalizes low-density lipoprotein particles through a calcium-dependent ectodomain. Multiple ligand-binding repeats capture lipoprotein cargo at the plasma membrane, while a downstream beta-propeller and adjacent EGF modules trigger pH-dependent cargo release in endosomes and enable receptor recycling. By driving endocytic uptake of lipoprotein cargo, it enhances cellular lipid handling and uptake pathways that feed into broader lipid transport systems.

A soluble oligomeric scaffold in Mycobacterium tuberculosis that assembles via homomeric interfaces to regulate carbohydrate flux through the pentose-phosphate pathway. Its isomerase-like fold supports strong self-association and complex formation, enabling assembly with metabolic enzymes and transient association with nucleic acid–proximal structures. This architecture positions the protein in the cytoplasm with regulated access to nuclear-like assemblies, where it likely coordinates ribose-phosphate and redox balance without relying on classical isomerase chemistry.

A multi-pass membrane cation channel that assembles as a tetramer and is gated by cyclic nucleotides. Its pore-forming core conducts ions, while a cytosolic cyclic nucleotide–binding module and a C-terminal leucine zipper coordinate allosteric gating and subunit assembly. The channel traffics through Golgi-associated vesicles and accumulates at the ciliary membrane, where its regulated cation flux supports ion transport and contributes to cilium assembly and signaling.

A cytoplasmic non-receptor tyrosine kinase that uses tandem phosphotyrosine-binding modules to dock onto receptor-proximal signaling assemblies and a C-terminal catalytic core to phosphorylate downstream targets. By coupling receptor engagement to phosphorylation of effectors such as phospholipase and adaptor hubs, it drives calcium mobilization and activates MAPK and NF-kappa-B pathways. This signaling hub operates near the cell cortex and in the cytoplasm to coordinate immune and hemostatic circuits, thereby tuning smooth muscle contractility, vascular tone, and renal system regulation through context-dependent pathway assembly.

A calcium-regulated phospholipase that hydrolyzes phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to generate diacylglycerol and inositol 1,4,5‑trisphosphate, thereby initiating lipid-derived signaling cascades. It operates as a cytoplasmic enzyme that transiently associates with the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane via membrane-targeting modules. Its pleckstrin homology and C2 domains position and stabilize the enzyme on phosphoinositide-rich surfaces, while EF-hand motifs and a regulatory C-terminal tail confer calcium sensitivity and coupling to heterotrimeric G protein pathways. Through this architecture, it drives second-messenger production and integrates GPCR inputs into localized signaling hubs.

A diacylglycerol-gated serine/threonine kinase that cycles between cytosol and membranes to coordinate signal transduction, apoptosis, and cytoskeletal control. Its N-terminal membrane-targeting modules recruit the enzyme to lipid microdomains where it phosphorylates substrates that regulate cell survival and motility. By assembling transient complexes with other enzymes and scaffolds, it both activates and organizes partner pathways, including acetylcholine receptor–coupled and postsynaptic signaling routes, consistent with a dynamic presence at the plasma membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, and cytoskeletal interfaces.

A multi-pass membrane cation channel that opens in response to cyclic nucleotides and assembles via a C-terminal leucine-zipper tail to form higher-order complexes. It mediates cation influx that supports membrane excitability and signaling, with prominent roles in the ciliary membrane where its activity contributes to assembly and maintenance of the cilium. Trafficking through Golgi-derived vesicles delivers the channel to the cell surface and ciliary compartment, where cyclic nucleotide binding allosterically gates the pore to tune ion transport.

A nuclear, sequence-specific DNA-binding regulator that uses a tandem array of zinc fingers to anchor at regulatory elements and assemble transcriptional complexes controlling hematopoietic programs. By homodimerizing and heterodimerizing with partner factors, it stabilizes occupancy at target sites and recruits chromatin-modifying assemblies to promote RNA polymerase II–dependent transcription in the appropriate cellular contexts.

A secreted glycosaminoglycan hydrolase in German yellow jacket venom that cleaves hyaluronan outside cells. By fragmenting extracellular matrix polymers through a TIM-barrel catalytic core, it reduces matrix viscosity and promotes tissue permeability, thereby facilitating venom dissemination and associated physiological effects during envenomation.

An ATP-driven RNA-termination machine in Neisseria gonorrhoeae that binds single-stranded RNA via an N-terminal RNA-recognition head and uses a central ATPase motor to translocate along transcripts, disengaging the elongation complex and enforcing transcription termination. It operates as a soluble cytoplasmic factor that coordinates with transcription and translation assemblies, using multivalent contacts to capture nascent RNA and couple ATP hydrolysis to efficient release of terminated messages.

A large cytoplasmic scaffold that organizes multivalent protein assemblies to regulate pathways underlying yeast community behavior. By coordinating cytoplasmic complexes that influence adhesin production, sorting, and display, it promotes biofilm formation on abiotic surfaces. Its extended adaptor architecture supports broad protein binding, enabling coupling of cytoskeletal and membrane-trafficking systems that collectively enhance surface adhesion and matrix-associated growth.

A soluble TPP-dependent oxidative decarboxylase in Nostoc that converts pyruvate-derived intermediates into reduced low-potential electron carriers. It binds thiamine pyrophosphate to generate and resolve a hydroxyethyl intermediate, then relays electrons through an internal iron–sulfur relay to ferredoxin or flavodoxin. By supplying reducing power to downstream pathways, it sustains cellular electron flow and integrates central carbon metabolism with redox bioenergetics. The enzyme operates predominantly in the cytoplasm but likely forms transient assemblies near membrane-associated redox hubs.

A soluble mitochondrial oxidoreductase that assembles a molybdenum-cofactor catalytic center and an internal cytochrome b5-like heme module to oxidize sulfur-containing substrates and funnel electrons into mitochondrial respiration. By coupling sulfur-group chemistry to electron transfer within the matrix, it supports energy metabolism and integrates sulfur flux with broader carbon utilization pathways through a dimeric scaffold that stabilizes cofactor binding and catalysis.

A single-pass membrane receptor with a large, calcium-stabilized extracellular scaffold that binds extracellular matrix and co-receptors to initiate endocytic uptake. Its modular ectodomain forms a pH-sensitive switch that captures ligands at the cell surface and releases them in endosomes, thereby driving receptor-mediated internalization and cargo trafficking from the plasma membrane.

A secreted glycoside hydrolase that cleaves extracellular hyaluronan into smaller fragments, thereby loosening matrix and enhancing the spread and efficacy of bee venom and antimicrobial factors. Built on a TIM-barrel catalytic core typical of hyaluronidases, it hydrolyzes β-linked polysaccharide bonds in the extracellular space, accelerating hyaluronan turnover and contributing to tissue permeability and innate defense.

A nuclear transcriptional activator that uses a basic-leucine zipper module to dimerize and bind promoter elements, thereby stimulating transcription of target genes. Its N-terminal activation region likely recruits coactivators and chromatin remodelers, enabling robust promoter occupancy and transcriptional output. This activity contributes to the activation of the alpha-glycoprotein gene by assembling an activation complex at its promoter and enhancing RNA polymerase II–mediated transcription.

A membrane-proximal signaling scaffold and kinase that concentrates at epithelial junctions and focal adhesions, where a large immunoglobulin-like ectodomain organizes adhesion complexes and the cytoplasmic kinase module transduces signals to remodel the actin cytoskeleton. By coupling adhesion cues to phosphorylation-driven pathways, it promotes epithelial junction formation and maintenance, supports cell migration and neurite outgrowth, and modulates morphogen and retinoid-responsive circuits through junction- and adhesion-centered assemblies.

A nuclear transcriptional regulator that uses a tandem array of zinc fingers to bind DNA and assemble chromatin-modifying complexes, thereby switching target genes between repression and activation. By anchoring to genomic sites and recruiting co-regulatory machinery, it shapes lineage-specific transcriptional programs, including those that drive antibody production and calcium-responsive pathways. Its mechanism centers on high-affinity DNA recognition by C2H2 fingers and context-dependent cofactor assembly that tunes gene expression in the nucleus.

An ER-resident, single-pass membrane Ca2+ sensor that orchestrates store-operated Ca2+ entry. Its N-terminal EF-hand detects ER Ca2+ status and triggers SAM domain–mediated oligomerization, exposing a C-terminal activating region that engages and gates plasma membrane Ca2+ channels. By coupling ER Ca2+ sensing to assembly of channel-regulatory complexes at ER–plasma membrane interfaces, it drives Ca2+ influx, sustains intracellular Ca2+ signaling, and supports diverse Ca2+-dependent cellular functions.

A cytoplasmic, calcium-regulated phosphodiesterase that hydrolyzes both cAMP and cGMP to their 5′-nucleotide products, thereby shaping intracellular cyclic-nucleotide signaling. An N-terminal regulatory module tunes a metallophosphohydrolase catalytic core, coupling calcium fluctuations to rapid clearance of cAMP/cGMP pools. Through this mechanism, the enzyme sculpts cytoplasmic signaling microdomains and terminates second-messenger pathways that drive downstream cellular responses.

A human epithelial adhesion receptor that forms desmosomal junctions at the cell surface. Its extracellular cadherin-like repeats bind calcium to rigidify adhesive interfaces, while the cytoplasmic tail recruits plaque proteins that anchor intermediate filaments. By assembling a robust membrane-embedded adhesion module, it mediates calcium-dependent cell-cell adhesion and contributes to epithelial tissue integrity and cornified envelope formation at the plasma membrane.

A large nuclear scaffold that assembles transcriptional and chromatin-associated complexes to restrain cell proliferation. Its extended MYM-type zinc-finger array and metal-tuned core create a high-avidity interaction platform, while a QRICH1-like C-terminal region stabilizes regulatory assemblies. By recruiting and organizing nuclear repression machinery, it dampens growth-promoting gene programs and enforces nuclear control over cell growth pathways.

A nucleocytoplasmic RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase that assembles via a central coiled-coil and uses a C‑terminal PRY/SPRY recognition module to recruit substrates and adaptors. By catalyzing ubiquitin transfer through its N‑terminal catalytic core and organizing higher-order assemblies, it modulates antiviral defense and broader stress pathways including apoptosis, autophagy, and DNA-damage responses. Its soluble architecture supports dynamic complexes in the cytoplasm and nucleus, where it fine-tunes signaling through selective ubiquitination.

A nucleolar SAM-dependent methyltransferase that assembles with ribosome-associated complexes to coordinate RNA maturation and assembly pathways that feed mitochondrial organization and energy supply. By operating as a multivalent assembly hub in the nucleolus, it helps tune ribosome biogenesis and cellular metabolism in ways that support mitochondrial architecture and, in germ cells, the energetic demands underlying motility. Its soluble architecture and nucleolar residency position it to scaffold protein–RNA assemblies that couple nucleolar function to broader cellular energy systems.

A DAG- and phorbol ester–activated serine/threonine kinase that orchestrates receptor- and G-protein–driven signaling. It is recruited to membranes by tandem lipid-sensing modules and a pleckstrin homology domain, where it becomes activated and phosphorylates downstream targets that regulate vesicle trafficking, cytoskeletal remodeling, and transcriptional programs. By cycling between cytosol, the trans-Golgi network, plasma membrane, and nucleus, it integrates membrane-proximal cues with hormone-responsive and innate defense pathways, including antimicrobial and antifungal responses.

A compact adaptor that organizes two major assemblies: a transcription-elongation module and a Cul2-based ubiquitin ligase. Its SKP1/POZ scaffold mediates high-affinity protein binding, stabilizing an elongation complex that supports processive RNA polymerase II and, in parallel, assembling cullin–RING ligase machinery that modifies target proteins. The protein shuttles between cytoplasm and nucleus, where it nucleates and maintains the elongin complex and participates in Cul2-dependent ubiquitination pathways through regulated partner recruitment and substrate-receptor engagement.

A ubiquitin-like adaptor that forms a stable platform for assembling transcription and ubiquitin-ligase machineries. It pairs with an elongation cofactor to stabilize RNA polymerase II–associated assemblies that drive transcript elongation and promoter-proximal events, while also nucleating cullin-based ubiquitin ligases that regulate targeted proteolysis. The protein operates in both cytoplasm and nucleus, with nuclear activity prominent during transcription, and functions by multivalent protein binding that organizes higher-order complexes rather than catalyzing chemistry.

A positive-sense RNA viral polyprotein that is proteolytically matured into structural and enzymatic components that build the virion and drive cytoplasmic RNA replication. Its N-terminal region forms the icosahedral shell, while central and C-terminal modules encode a helicase and an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that assemble replication factories. A chymotrypsin-like protease core processes the polyprotein and also edits host ubiquitin chains, thereby dampening innate immune and Toll-like receptor pathways. Together, these activities coordinate virion assembly, genome replication, and immune suppression within the host cytoplasm and virion.

A soluble human ubiquitin-like modifier that operates in the cytoplasm to covalently attach to lysine residues on target proteins through an isopeptide-bond mechanism. By using a compact β-grasp fold to assemble and stabilize conjugation complexes, it drives reversible modification events that regulate target stability and signaling pathways, particularly through neddylation cycles that tune cytoplasmic protein assemblies.

A mitochondrial inner-membrane–associated redox enzyme that accepts electrons from soluble metabolic carriers and transfers them through a flavin- and iron–sulfur-based relay to reduce ubiquinone in the respiratory chain. Its architecture couples a soluble redox core to a membrane-proximal quinone-binding site, enabling efficient electron flow from upstream donors to the ubiquinone pool and thereby sustaining oxidative energy conversion within mitochondria.

A soluble human oxygenase that converts cysteine to sulfide and L-alanine in the cytoplasm. It uses a cupin/jelly-roll scaffold to coordinate a ferrous cofactor that activates molecular oxygen and drives cysteine dioxygenation, thereby supplying hydrogen sulfide for signaling and metabolism. The active site can also bind zinc, which likely modulates stability or inhibition. By coupling oxygen insertion chemistry to sulfur amino acid turnover, it feeds cytosolic sulfide pathways and integrates with broader sulfur and redox metabolism.

A basolateral, multi-pass membrane transporter that uses the inward sodium gradient to drive concentrative uptake of monocarboxylates, notably lactate and pyruvate, and likely ketone bodies. By coupling sodium binding to substrate translocation through an alternating-access mechanism, it supports vectorial transport and metabolic exchange across polarized epithelial and endothelial surfaces, aligning with basolateral localization and energized monocarboxylate handling.

A soluble mouse enzyme that catalyzes the decarboxylation step producing quinolinic acid and thereby feeds into broader aromatic metabolite biosynthesis. Its fold and chemistry align with a cofactor-independent decarboxylase that operates efficiently in the peroxisomal matrix, where import via peroxisomal targeting machinery positions the enzyme to protect labile intermediates and coordinate carbon and redox balance. By converting an oxo–hydroxy–ureidoimidazoline intermediate to quinolinic acid, it supplies a key node that supports downstream aromatic pathway assembly.

A modular transcriptional co-regulator that assembles with TEAD transcription factors via an N‑terminal docking element and uses tandem WW repeats to recruit additional regulators, thereby tuning gene-expression programs that remodel the cytoskeleton and control cell morphology. It shuttles between cytoplasm and nucleus, integrating upstream signaling cues to coordinate cytoskeletal organization and cell-shape regulation through TEAD-dependent transcriptional outputs.

A soluble effector from an intracellular apicomplexan-derived bacterium that uses multivalent protein binding to remodel host pathways. By assembling and modulating host complexes, it suppresses inflammatory signaling, interferes with autophagy and xenophagy, and promotes intracellular persistence. Its activity culminates in the host nucleus, where it likely tunes transcriptional programs and chromatin-associated responses that determine cell survival and immune evasion.

A membrane-embedded acyltransferase that installs palmitate onto diverse cysteine residues of client proteins to control their membrane affinity, trafficking, and signaling competence. By forming a transient acyl–enzyme intermediate at the cytosolic face of membranes, it drives palmitoylation that stabilizes immune receptor pathways and enhances their surface residency, thereby promoting innate immune signaling and the delivery of proteins to the plasma membrane. The same mechanism operates in neurons to tune dendritic signaling and within phagocytic vesicles to coordinate receptor and adaptor dynamics.

A soluble serine hydrolase in Aspergillus that uses an alpha/beta hydrolase catalytic core to hydrolyze ester bonds in a lipase-like manner. By mobilizing acyl pools, it contributes to primary lipid turnover and supplies acyl flux that supports secondary-metabolite assembly lines, including pathways that produce mycotoxins. The enzyme likely operates in the cytosol while transiently associating with organelle-proximal metabolons, where its acyl–ester chemistry helps gate flux through toxin biosynthesis.

A soluble bacterial nuclease that forms homodimers, binds double-stranded DNA, and cleaves it at defined sites to drive restriction–modification defense and DNA-damage signaling. By generating endonucleolytic breaks that both sample and degrade invasive DNA, it initiates pathways culminating in the SOS response and coordinates with cytoplasmic DNA repair and recombination machinery.

A lipid-guided adaptor that uses tandem pleckstrin-homology modules to bind anionic membranes and assemble signaling and RNA-regulatory complexes. By docking to phosphatidylserine-, phosphoinositide-, and cardiolipin-rich surfaces, it shuttles between the cytoplasm and mitochondrial membranes, where it promotes hypoxia-responsive apoptosis and couples to cytoskeletal interfaces. The scaffold represses translation by driving selective mRNA decay through 3'-UTR pathways and thereby coordinates stress-induced cell-fate decisions with mitochondrial signaling hubs.

A multi-pass membrane transporter in mouse epithelia and neurons that harnesses the inward sodium gradient to drive high-affinity uptake of monocarboxylates—most prominently lactate and pyruvate—thereby concentrating organic acids for energy metabolism and redox balance. Its transmembrane symporter core cycles through alternating-access states to couple Na+ binding to substrate translocation at the cell surface of kidney and brain-associated tissues, supporting epithelial and neuronal physiology through sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transport.

A small accessory subunit of mitochondrial complex I that resides on the matrix-exposed face of the inner membrane and stabilizes the peripheral arm of the NADH-to-ubiquinone electron-transfer pathway. By reinforcing assembly and structural integrity rather than catalysis, it sustains efficient electron flow that fuels respiratory energy production. Its soluble, peripheral membrane profile positions it at the inner membrane where it supports the larger oxidative enzyme system that drives mitochondrial bioenergetics.

A large Ig-like scaffold that assembles and stabilizes axonemal and basal body complexes required for motile cilia and flagella. By providing multivalent binding surfaces, it organizes the structural modules that build and maintain the axoneme, thereby enabling coordinated ciliary and flagellar beating. It operates within the axoneme and associated cytoskeletal pools, where it nucleates higher-order assemblies that couple axoneme assembly to efficient motility.

A nucleocytoplasmic deubiquitinating enzyme that assembles via an N-terminal adaptor platform to recruit ubiquitinated substrates and chromatin targets, then uses a papain-like catalytic center to hydrolyze ubiquitin from proteins and histones. By reversing ubiquitin marks, it stabilizes or remodels client proteins, edits histone ubiquitination to tune transcriptional and circadian pathways, and engages pathway-specific partners through a dedicated binding module that broadens substrate scope and regulates activity across cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments.

A large cytoplasmic assembly-line enzyme that activates carboxylate substrates with ATP and channels them on internal carrier domains to build siderophore-associated metabolites during iron limitation. Its adenylation core and internal carrier modules cooperate to load and shuttle intermediates through a condensation-centered catalytic scaffold, enabling ATP-dependent activation, thiolation, and tailoring chemistry that supports iron-acquisition pathways. The chemistry likely includes acyl transfer and derivatization steps that can encompass methylation within a broader secondary-metabolite program responsive to iron starvation.

A lipolytic α/β-hydrolase in Aspergillus fumigatus that hydrolyzes acyl-ester intermediates within a membrane-associated biosynthetic assembly driving dehydroabietinal formation and the production of abietinal and downstream mycotoxins such as gliotoxin and fumigones. Its catalytic triad and oxyanion-stabilized core enable triglyceride and ceramide esterase chemistry, thereby editing hydrophobic pathway intermediates and channeling flux through a vesicle- or ER-proximal metabolon that supports secondary metabolite biosynthesis.

A soluble metallo–aminopeptidase that assembles into homomeric complexes and trims N-terminal residues from extracellular peptides and proteins. By shaping the pericellular peptide landscape through metal-dependent aminopeptidase chemistry, it likely tunes reproductive cues that facilitate single fertilization events. Its oligomeric assembly and absence of transmembrane features support action in the extracellular milieu of gametes or surrounding tissues.

A soluble, thiamine-dependent oxidoreductase in Rhodospirillum rubrum that decarboxylates pyruvate and channels the resulting electrons through internal relay elements to ferredoxin or flavodoxin. By coupling TPP-driven decarboxylation to iron–sulfur-mediated electron transfer, it supplies low-potential reducing power that feeds cellular electron-transport pathways and central carbon metabolism. The enzyme operates predominantly in the cytoplasm but can transiently associate with membrane-proximal redox assemblies and extracytoplasmic compartments via protein docking.

A soluble bacterial nuclease–helicase that forms an ATP-fueled degradation machine for invasive DNA. Its N-terminal metal-binding nuclease initiates cleavage, while a central helicase engine uses nucleotide hydrolysis to unwind and feed DNA. A Cas3-specific C-terminal region stabilizes oligomerization and couples motor motion to cutting. Operating predominantly in the cytoplasm, it collaborates with CRISPR surveillance assemblies to processively dismantle target DNA during adaptive defense.

A peripheral membrane regulator that assembles as a homodimeric CBS-domain scaffold to control antibiotic production and release in Brachyspira. Its tandem CBS core provides an allosteric switch that organizes oligomeric assemblies, while a downstream transporter-associated scaffold anchors the complex near the outer membrane. Through ligand-responsive conformational changes, it coordinates the assembly and trafficking steps that culminate in metribenzylic acid biosynthesis and secretion.

A nuclear developmental regulator in Aspergillus nidulans that assembles via a velvet-domain core into higher-order complexes controlling light-responsive pathways, secondary metabolism, and developmental decisions. By forming symmetric oligomers that recruit transcriptional and chromatin-associated machinery, it orchestrates sporulation and cell differentiation and likely enforces nuclear programs that indirectly suppress viral RNA replication. Its mechanism centers on velvet-domain–mediated self-association and assembly of regulatory hubs that tune gene-expression states during fungal development.

A cytoplasmic adaptor that uses tandem SH3 modules to assemble multiprotein complexes controlling actin remodeling and membrane-proximal pathways. By scaffolding cytoskeletal and endocytic factors, it organizes cell architecture and morphology, stimulates ectodomain shedding events, and promotes routes that enhance protein turnover. It predominantly resides in the cytoplasm with a secondary nuclear pool, where transient shuttling likely coordinates gene-expression modules that tune cytoskeletal and proteolytic programs.

A seven-helix chemosensory receptor in human cells that resides in the plasma membrane and transduces extracellular bitter/umami cues into intracellular signals via heterotrimeric G proteins. By activating canonical GPCR pathways, it modulates downstream effectors that fine-tune excitability and can suppress transporter and ion-transport systems during taste perception. Its multi-pass architecture creates a ligand-binding cavity and a cytosolic signaling surface that engages G proteins and regulatory factors to coordinate signal amplitude and duration.

A soluble flavoenzyme that uses a FAD/NAD(P)-binding core to mediate reversible redox between chromophore and 2‑hydroxychromophore during anaerobic degradation of aromatic amino acids. By accepting hydride from NADPH and relaying it through a flavin cofactor, it drives a key reductive step that stabilizes pathway intermediates en route to ring‑modified products central to phenylalanine and related amino acid metabolism. The enzyme functions in the soluble compartment of the cell, where it coordinates with other redox and aromatic‑ring–transforming enzymes to balance electron flow during denitrification pathways.

A soluble bacterial termination factor that binds nascent single-stranded RNA through an N-terminal OB-fold platform and uses an ATP-driven motor to remodel and disengage the elongation complex, thereby enforcing rapid transcript release during transcription. Its RNA-binding and ATPase modules operate in tandem to couple RNA capture with mechanical translocation, positioning the factor at the hub of termination and broader RNA-handling pathways in the cytoplasm.

A large human nuclear regulator that assembles multivalent protein–protein interaction hubs to control transcriptional programs linked to cell shape and movement. Its central MYM-type zinc-finger array and metal-coordination core create high-capacity binding surfaces that recruit chromatin-modifying and remodeling assemblies, thereby tuning expression of pathways that organize the cytoskeleton and govern morphogenesis. Operating within the nucleus, it likely functions as a scaffold that couples epigenetic repression and activation to downstream remodeling of cellular architecture.

A human multi-pass membrane acyltransferase that installs reversible fatty acyl groups onto cysteine residues of membrane-proximal proteins, thereby tuning their membrane affinity, trafficking, and signaling. It operates through a DHHC-centered catalytic cycle that forms an acyl-enzyme intermediate to transfer palmitate and, with lower specificity, other acyl chains such as myristate and stearate. By controlling the acylation state of diverse clients at the plasma membrane and along the secretory/endocytic pathway, it orchestrates membrane residency and pathway selection for key signaling and trafficking factors.

A multi-pass membrane acyltransferase in mouse that installs palmitate onto cysteine residues of diverse cytosolic and membrane-associated proteins. By forming a transient acyl–enzyme intermediate, it drives both constitutive and regulated palmitoylation, thereby increasing substrate hydrophobicity and promoting their membrane association and trafficking. This activity supports the palmitoylation of soluble tubulin dimers and contributes to establishing protein localization at the plasma membrane, consistent with residence across intracellular organelles and the cell surface.

A soluble cytosolic enzyme that uses a thiamine diphosphate–dependent mechanism to transfer two-carbon units between sugar phosphates, thereby driving non-oxidative rearrangements that balance flux through the pentose phosphate pathway. Its N-terminal catalytic scaffold and central pyrimidine-binding core assemble a metal-stabilized active site that binds thiamine diphosphate and executes reversible ketol-group transfer. Dimerization at the C-terminus completes the active-site architecture and supports efficient catalysis, coupling cofactor and metal binding to sustain nucleotide precursor and redox homeostasis in the cytoplasm.

A DAG-activated serine/threonine kinase that cycles between cytosol and peripheral membrane via tandem lipid-sensing modules. Upon diacylglycerol engagement, it relocates to membrane microdomains, assembles signaling scaffolds, and phosphorylates cytosolic targets to coordinate vesicle trafficking, cytoskeletal remodeling, and signal relay that ultimately modulates nuclear import pathways. Its N-terminal regulatory and scaffolding surfaces organize partner binding, while a C-terminal catalytic core executes phosphorylation to couple membrane-proximal cues to nuclear transport control.

A multi-pass membrane cation channel that assembles as a homotetramer and is gated by cyclic nucleotides. Its pore-forming core conducts monovalent and divalent cations, while a C-terminal cyclic nucleotide–binding module and leucine-zipper assembly domain tune gating and stabilize oligomerization. The channel operates predominantly at the ciliary membrane and traffics through Golgi-derived vesicles, where its ion-conducting activity and scaffolding roles help establish local cation microdomains that support cilium biogenesis and signaling.

A soluble, calcium-regulated phosphodiesterase that hydrolyzes both cAMP and cGMP to terminate cyclic nucleotide signaling. Its N-terminal regulatory module engages calcium–calmodulin to allosterically activate a metallo-hydrolase catalytic core, thereby shaping local second-messenger gradients that control secretion and sensory transduction. Operating predominantly in the cytoplasm and concentrated within signaling cilia, it dampens cyclic nucleotide pathways that modulate insulin release and olfactory signal processing, with trafficking through endolysosomal compartments contributing to turnover and localization.

A cytoplasmic, calcium-responsive cyclic-nucleotide phosphodiesterase that hydrolyzes both cAMP and cGMP. An N-terminal regulatory module couples Ca2+-calmodulin signals to a metallo-hydrolase catalytic core, enabling tight control of cyclic-nucleotide turnover. By locally shaping second-messenger gradients, it tunes neuronal signaling pathways that underlie olfactory transduction and broader cAMP/cGMP-dependent processes.

A cytoplasmic, cortex-enriched non-receptor tyrosine kinase that uses tandem phosphotyrosine-binding modules to assemble at membrane-proximal signaling hubs and activate a C‑terminal catalytic core. By docking onto phosphorylated adaptors and receptors, it relieves autoinhibition to phosphorylate nearby substrates that govern immune and cytoskeletal pathways. This signaling hub modulates smooth muscle contractility and vascular tone, integrates secretion and renal system regulation, and coordinates broader cellular responses through dynamic localization in the cytoplasm and at the cell cortex.

A nucleo-cytoplasmic deubiquitinating enzyme that assembles via an N-terminal adaptor platform and a central papain-like catalytic core to remove ubiquitin from diverse substrates. By stabilizing key clock repressors and chromatin-associated targets, it tunes circadian timing and modulates protein turnover and transcriptional programs. The enzyme operates in both cytoplasm and nucleus, where modular interaction domains recruit circadian and chromatin regulators and position substrates for precise isopeptide hydrolysis.

A membrane-associated cytochrome P450 monooxygenase in yeast that catalyzes key oxidative tailoring steps within a secondary metabolite pathway culminating in mycotoxin formation. Anchored to intracellular membranes, it binds a heme cofactor and uses electron transfer to insert oxygen into hydrophobic intermediates, thereby driving the late-stage transformations that complete toxin assembly. Its membrane-proximal positioning and reliance on soluble redox partners enable efficient channeling of pathway intermediates toward the final product.

A large cytosolic nuclease-helicase that forms the catalytic core of a bacterial adaptive defense system. It uses a metal-dependent nuclease center to cleave nucleic acids and an ATP-driven helicase engine to unwind and translocate along nucleic acid substrates. By assembling into processive nucleoprotein filaments, it degrades invasive nucleic acids and promotes strand exchange and recombination intermediates that underpin adaptive immunity in the bacterial cytoplasm.

A nuclear transcriptional regulator in Arabidopsis that uses a NAC DNA-binding module to recognize specific promoter elements and assemble repressive complexes that fine-tune gene expression. By enforcing chromatin-mediated repression through its C-terminal effector region, it dampens basal transcription yet coordinates antifungal defense pathways. Its activity is centered in the nucleus, where it integrates stress signals to modulate immune-responsive transcriptional networks.

A multivalent scaffold that builds and stabilizes the intraflagellar transport A complex to drive cargo movement within zebrafish cilia. Its tandem beta-propeller core and extended repeat architecture create high-affinity binding surfaces that assemble IFT particles, enabling retrograde trafficking and supporting cilium assembly and cargo delivery. It concentrates at the basal body with a cytoplasmic pool and likely couples IFT assemblies to ciliary motors to maintain and localize proteins within the cilium.

A cytosolic, vesicle-associated signaling enzyme that assembles via armadillo and sterile alpha motif modules to form higher-order arrays that activate a C-terminal signaling core. Through self-association, it concentrates and activates NAD+ cleavage chemistry, thereby degrading cellular NAD+ and generating signals that tune innate immune and stress-response pathways. It operates primarily in the cytoplasm but associates with cytoplasmic vesicle membranes and vacuolar membranes, where endomembrane signaling and cargo trafficking provide the platform for its oligomerization-coupled enzymatic mechanism.

A nuclear scaffold that integrates a WD40 β-propeller with a C-terminal acetyl-lysine–recognition module to assemble chromatin-tethered regulatory complexes. By anchoring to acetylated nucleosomes and recruiting transcriptional and cell-cycle factors, it organizes nuclear assemblies that tune developmental and checkpoint pathways. This reader–scaffold mechanism positions the protein to modulate programs that culminate in sporulation-like outcomes under specialized conditions.

A cytoplasmic signaling enzyme that assembles into higher-order complexes to hydrolyze NAD+ into ADP-ribose and nicotinamide. Its armadillo-repeat scaffold and polymerizing module organize and concentrate the catalytic core, which drives nucleotide catabolism that reshapes neuronal fate decisions. By collapsing NAD+ pools and generating ADP-ribose, it promotes pathways that regulate dendrite architecture and can tilt neurons toward apoptosis and cell death. The assemblies predominantly reside in the cytoplasm but can access the nucleus during stress-responsive signaling.

A cytoplasmic RNA-binding protein that uses a La-type winged-helix core followed by tandem RNA-recognition motifs to bind adenosine-rich single-stranded RNA and assemble ribonucleoprotein complexes. By stabilizing mRNA–ribosome assemblies and coupling them to cytoskeletal platforms, it enhances translational output and coordinates mRNA handling with filament dynamics that shape cell morphology. Its soluble architecture and partnerships with cytoskeletal and ribosome-associated factors position it within higher-order assemblies that integrate translation with cytoskeleton organization.

A large, multi-pass membrane regulator in fruit fly that adopts a rhomboid-like fold but functions primarily as a non-catalytic scaffold. Embedded in endoplasmic reticulum membranes, it assembles oligomeric complexes that bind client proteins and adaptors to tune membrane-protein maturation and trafficking. By constraining the biogenesis and routing of growth factor receptors, it dampens downstream signaling and biases neuronal and endocrine circuits that shape sleep/wake cycles and circadian timing. Transient interfaces with nuclear-proximal pathways likely couple ER-centered regulation to transcriptional programs.

A mitochondrial initiation-factor scaffold that binds the small ribosomal subunit and initiator tRNA to assemble and stabilize the initiation complex for organellar protein synthesis. By tuning mitoribosome dynamics and start-site selection, it promotes accurate initiation and thereby drives mitochondrial translation from within the matrix, where it transiently associates with the mitoribosome and initiation machinery.

A mitochondrial redox hub that associates peripherally with the inner membrane to relay electrons from soluble flavoprotein pathways and acyl‑CoA dehydrogenases into the ubiquinone pool. By binding a flavin cofactor and positioning ubiquinone for reduction, it sustains electron flow during fatty acid breakdown and thereby supports respiratory energy production in the organelle.

A soluble mitochondrial adaptor that suppresses apoptosis by assembling and stabilizing survival-promoting complexes at or near mitochondria. Its architecture indicates a non-enzymatic scaffold that binds other proteins to modulate mitochondrial checkpoints in cell death, thereby dampening pro-apoptotic signaling and supporting survival pathways, including those co-opted during symbiont-driven inhibition of host apoptosis.

A cytoplasmic, oligomeric M17-family aminopeptidase that assembles into higher-order complexes to regulate intracellular peptide turnover and tune developmental signaling pathways required for mesoderm formation. Its N-terminal assembly module and C-terminal catalytic core cooperate to create a metallo-exopeptidase platform that trims N-terminal residues from peptides while scaffolding self-association and transient interactions. Operating within the cytoplasm and at the surfaces of membrane-bounded organelles, it likely modulates signaling thresholds that guide mesodermal patterning.

A membrane-proximal serine/threonine kinase that organizes polarity and cytoskeletal systems by phosphorylating microtubule-associated and polarity regulators. Its N-terminal catalytic core performs serine/threonine phosphorylation, a central ubiquitin-associated module recruits ubiquitin-marked partners and substrates, and a C-terminal KA1 tether anchors the enzyme to membrane-associated cytoskeletal hubs. Through spatially controlled phosphorylation, it activates downstream pathways that stabilize microtubules, promote axon extension, and coordinate actin dynamics to establish neuronal and epithelial polarity.

A soluble, cytoplasmic thiamine diphosphate–dependent two-carbon transferase that assembles into a multimeric enzyme to interconvert sugar phosphates in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway. Its N-terminal catalytic scaffold and central thiamine diphosphate pocket cooperate with C-terminal stabilizing domains to generate and channel intermediates that balance ribose-5-phosphate supply and carbon rearrangement. Magnesium or manganese coordinates the cofactor to tune catalysis, and transient association with nucleoid-proximal metabolism likely explains occasional nuclear-adjacent localization.

A soluble α/β-hydrolase enzyme in Neurospora crassa that catalyzes acyl- and ester-handling steps within the ochratoxin pathway. By forming and resolving acyl-enzyme intermediates, it provides both hydrolysis and acyl-transfer chemistry that remodels acetylated and xanthate-bearing intermediates en route to the neurotoxic polyketide. The enzyme likely operates in the cytoplasm and transiently associates with membrane-bounded compartments that organize secondary-metabolite assembly lines, thereby channeling flux toward ochratoxin production.

A multi-pass membrane receptor in mouse that uses a seven-helix transmembrane core to sense extracellular chemosensory cues and convert them into intracellular signals. By adopting an active conformation that engages heterotrimeric G proteins, it initiates canonical second-messenger cascades associated with taste-related signaling and related pathways. Its membrane-embedded architecture positions extracellular loops for ligand capture and intracellular loops for partner recruitment, enabling modulation by lipid-like molecules and assembly of transient signaling complexes at the cell surface.

A large mouse scaffold that combines an N-terminal leucine-rich repeat array with a C-terminal PDZ module to assemble membrane-proximal signaling and cytoskeletal complexes. By capturing the cytoplasmic tails of membrane proteins and coupling them to cytoskeletal adaptors, it organizes postsynaptic assemblies that tune neurotransmitter receptor abundance at excitatory synapses and supports polarized basolateral membrane organization. The same multivalent platform sequesters and modulates innate immune receptor pathways, dampening downstream signaling and chemokine output. It resides predominantly at the cytoplasm–cytoskeleton interface and the plasma membrane, where it directs protein targeting and spatial organization of receptor and signaling networks.

A membrane-associated lipid-transfer scaffold in mouse that concentrates at endoplasmic reticulum–plasma membrane junctions. An N-terminal lipid-sensing module anchors the protein to specific membrane interfaces, while a C-terminal sterol-binding module captures and shuttles cholesterol between apposed membranes. Through regulated, non-vesicular transfer, it stabilizes cellular cholesterol balance and tunes membrane composition at contact sites, coordinating with ER tethers and lipid-transfer hubs to maintain sterol homeostasis.

A Golgi-resident, single-pass type II membrane enzyme that transfers sulfate from PAPS onto heparan sulfate chains during proteoglycan assembly. Its luminal catalytic domain modifies glycosaminoglycans within the secretory pathway, shaping the sulfation patterns that govern ligand binding and signaling. By operating in the Golgi membrane with a nucleotide-cofactor–binding core, it drives a key step of heparan sulfate proteoglycan biosynthesis and coordinates with neighboring glycan-modifying enzymes to achieve ordered chain maturation.

A large Ig-like repeat scaffold in mouse that assembles and stabilizes axonemal protein complexes required for motile cilium and flagellum function. Operating as a multivalent adaptor rather than an enzyme, it concentrates within the axoneme after cytoplasmic and cytoskeletal assembly, where it promotes axoneme construction and tunes motility. By organizing partner modules that build and regulate the ciliary shaft, it supports beat mechanics and links ciliary assembly to broader motility-dependent physiology.

A soluble bacterial transcriptional regulator that binds promoter-proximal DNA via an N‑terminal helix–turn–helix winged-helix domain and uses a C‑terminal effector-binding module to tune oligomerization and promoter activation. By assembling on operator sites and shaping local DNA architecture, it stimulates transcription of operons linked to extracellular matrix and polysaccharide pathways in Pseudomonas fluorescens, functioning within nucleoid-associated protein–DNA assemblies to positively regulate gene expression in response to small-molecule signals.

A soluble cytoplasmic dehydrogenase that binds NAD and NADP via an N-terminal Rossmann-like core and uses a C-terminal catalytic module to oxidize acetaldehyde to acetyl-CoA. By coupling aldehyde oxidation to cofactor-driven hydride transfer, it detoxifies acetaldehyde and feeds acetyl units into central metabolism. This activity integrates into bacterial pathways that degrade aromatic compounds, likely operating within transient cytosolic assemblies that channel reactive aldehydes toward energy and biosynthetic pathways.

A soluble cytosolic pyrophosphohydrolase that uses a NUDIX catalytic core to hydrolyze nucleoside diphosphate–linked metabolites, including ADP-ribose, NADH/NAD+, and dinucleoside oligomers. By clearing these reactive nucleotide species, it stabilizes cytosolic nucleotide and redox pools that feed into glycoprotein biogenesis, thereby supporting N-linked glycosylation. Its soluble architecture and lack of transmembrane segments place it in the cytoplasm, where it couples metabolic state to glycosylation efficiency through targeted pyrophosphate bond hydrolysis.

An outer-membrane-associated scaffold that organizes lipoprotein transport and surface-protein maturation in Bacteroides. It assembles into higher-order complexes at the cell envelope, where it binds partner proteins and promotes homotrimerization to build a membrane-proximal platform. By clustering client proteins and processing enzymes at the outer membrane and adjacent peptidoglycan layer, it facilitates lipoprotein trafficking and proteolytic activation steps that collectively shape the bacterial surface.

A cyclophilin-like foldase anchored at the bacterial outer membrane that accelerates cis-trans isomerization of proline bonds to drive efficient folding and assembly of envelope-associated proteins. By catalyzing a key rate-limiting step in maturation, it supports de novo protein folding and quality control of outer-membrane clients, stabilizing the assembly of surface complexes and channels at the cell envelope interface.

A homomeric adhesin that assembles via an N-terminal scaffold and a large beta-propeller platform to mediate high-avidity attachment in a host-associated niche. It likely oligomerizes to increase binding avidity and promotes bacterial adhesion and colonization. The protein is synthesized and assembled in the cytoplasm and is routed through endoplasmic reticulum–linked pathways en route to surface display, enabling firm engagement with host-derived substrates.

An outer-membrane assembly machine that uses an N-terminal periplasmic scaffold to capture and organize β-barrel precursors and chaperones, and a C-terminal β-barrel platform that transiently gates a channel to drive membrane insertion. By orchestrating outer-membrane biogenesis, it shapes envelope integrity and indirectly influences lysis-associated pathways and host-membrane remodeling typical of symbiotic and phage-interactive lifestyles. It resides in the bacterial outer membrane with a large periplasmic domain and functions through multivalent client binding and a gated insertion mechanism.

A periplasm-facing outer-membrane lipoprotein that forms homooligomeric rings and serves as an assembly factor for outer-membrane protein biogenesis. Its helical repeat scaffold creates a multivalent binding platform that organizes and stabilizes the outer-membrane assembly machinery, particularly in concert with the periplasmic assembly factor that drives substrate insertion. By coordinating complex assembly at the bacterial outer membrane, it supports efficient maturation and insertion of outer-membrane proteins.

A cytoplasmic scaffold that oligomerizes through a BTB/POZ core to assemble ubiquitin-ligase–associated complexes that restrain RhoA signaling and stabilize neuronal cytoskeletons. By organizing higher-order assemblies that likely recruit cullin-based machinery, it dampens RhoA-driven actomyosin dynamics, thereby supporting dendritic architecture and enhancing synaptic transmission. The complex operates in the cytoplasm and along cytoskeletal structures, where multivalent self-association concentrates client proteins for efficient regulation.

A single-pass membrane receptor-like signaling protein in mouse that presents a large extracellular immunoglobulin scaffold for adhesion and ligand capture and a cytosolic kinase module that assembles phosphorylation-dependent signaling complexes. By concentrating at the plasma membrane, cell–cell junctions, and focal adhesions, it couples extracellular cues to intracellular pathways that remodel the actin cytoskeleton, drive cell migration, and promote neurite and axon development. Its adhesion-tuned signaling platform potentiates pathways such as canonical Wnt and integrates morphogen inputs like retinoic acid to coordinate tissue remodeling and neuronal projection growth.

A multi-pass membrane transporter in mouse that uses a major facilitator architecture to move neutral and essential branched-chain amino acids across the plasma membrane. By coupling ion gradients to an alternating-access mechanism, it mediates uptake of isoleucine, leucine, and valine, thereby sustaining cellular amino acid supply and feeding into anabolic and nutrient-sensing pathways at the cell surface.

A soluble cytosolic dipeptidase that operates as a metallo-dependent homodimer to hydrolyze diverse dipeptides, with a preference for cysteinylglycine and efficient turnover of substrates such as carnosine and hydroxylysine. By clearing dipeptide end-products in the cytoplasm, it supports glutathione pathway flux and redox balance. The catalytic mechanism relies on a divalent metal coordinated by conserved residues within a metallo-enzyme core, with dimerization shaping the active-site architecture and substrate scope.

A cytoplasmic RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase that assembles into dimers and higher-order scaffolds to ubiquitinate cytoplasmic targets. Its N-terminal catalytic module drives ubiquitin transfer, central coiled-coil stabilizes active oligomers, and a C-terminal PRY/SPRY platform confers selective substrate binding. By decorating RNA-associated and signaling proteins with ubiquitin, it modulates RNA–protein assemblies and innate immune pathways, thereby coordinating cytoplasmic protein quality control and signaling dynamics.

A multi-pass plasma membrane ion channel that converts membrane tension into cation influx, thereby elevating cytosolic calcium and initiating mechanotransduction pathways. Its N-terminal and distal transmembrane assemblies form a tension-gated pore that drives calcium entry and broader ion transport, coordinating membrane-associated signaling and trafficking events that establish cellular localization dynamics at the cell surface.

A membrane-proximal small GTPase switch that cycles between GTP- and GDP-bound states to control actin remodeling and membrane dynamics central to innate immune functions. By assembling effector complexes at the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane and within the cytoplasm, it orchestrates protrusion, endocytosis, and phagocytic pathways that support defense against Gram-negative bacteria and broader innate immune responses.

A multi-pass plasma membrane transporter in mouse that uses a major facilitator superfamily fold to shuttle neutral and hydrophobic amino acids across the lipid bilayer. It mediates uptake of branched-chain and aromatic amino acids—including isoleucine, valine, and phenylalanine—with additional capacity for methionine and tyrosine. By cycling through alternating-access states likely energized by the proton gradient, it supports epithelial amino acid acquisition and broader nutrient homeostasis at the cell surface.

A soluble SAM-dependent arginine methyltransferase that assembles into higher-order complexes to symmetrically dimethylate arginine residues on histones and diverse RNA-binding proteins. By coupling chromatin modification with assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins, it coordinates nuclear and cytoplasmic pathways that drive snRNP biogenesis, pre-mRNA splicing, and transcriptional control. Its multimeric scaffold recruits substrates and cofactors to tune cell-cycle and p53-related signaling, and it operates in both nucleus and cytoplasm as part of larger protein assemblies.

A seven-transmembrane chemosensory receptor in mouse that resides at the cell surface and transduces extracellular cues into intracellular signals via heterotrimeric G proteins. Its rhodopsin-like core binds small organic and biogenic molecules, initiating pathways that regulate neuronal and epithelial signaling. By coupling extracellular stimuli—including salts and nitrogen-containing metabolites—to intracellular second messengers, it modulates excitability and secretory programs characteristic of sensory and enteric circuits.

A cytoplasmic actin-based motor that uses an ATP-driven myosin head to bind and remodel actin filaments, generating force and directed movement that shape protrusive and cortical assemblies in malaria parasites. By coupling nucleotide hydrolysis to mechanical output, it concentrates at actin-rich structures and filopodia-like projections, where it powers local tension and transport essential for cytoskeletal dynamics and intracellular trafficking.

A calmodulin-like adaptor that uses a tandem EF-hand module to sense calcium and regulate partner binding, thereby organizing actin–myosin assemblies that underpin the parasite’s pellicle. By coupling to myosin-associated complexes and tuning their interactions with actin and membrane-cytoskeletal linkers, it stabilizes and remodels filament systems essential for cell shape and motility within the pellicle layer.

A nuclear transcriptional regulator in fruit fly that combines an N-terminal LIM zinc-finger scaffold with a central homeodomain to assemble multiprotein complexes and anchor them to regulatory DNA. By recruiting cofactors through the LIM module and engaging target enhancers via the homeodomain, it modulates gene expression programs that drive tissue patterning and organogenesis, including pathways influencing root morphogenesis.

A cytoplasmic scaffold that assembles into higher-order complexes to coordinate intracellular trafficking and endocytosis. By forming homotetrameric coiled-coil assemblies, it recruits and organizes membrane-trafficking machinery at the surface of intracellular organelles, thereby promoting vesicle-mediated transport and cargo internalization. Through this trafficking control, it indirectly drives cell migration and chemotaxis by regulating receptor and membrane recycling pathways.

A human multi-pass membrane transporter–like protein that assembles with trafficking machinery to coordinate leucine-dependent pathways. Its SLC35F-class architecture and EmrE-like core create a stable membrane scaffold that primarily operates through protein binding to cargo-sorting modules at the endolysosomal/vacuolar interface. By coupling leucine handling to vesicle sorting and autophagic routes, it tunes membrane trafficking and degradative pathways that respond to amino acid availability.

A large cytoplasmic RNA-remodeling enzyme that uses an ATP-driven helicase core to bind and unwind structured viral and cellular RNAs, thereby assembling and potentiating cytoplasmic antiviral signaling complexes. By capturing RNA through an N-terminal PIN-like module and coordinating remodeling with a C-terminal winged-helix platform, it promotes antiviral defense and enhances RNA-sensing pathways that lead to interferon responses. Its RNA-centric remodeling role also links to broader RNA surveillance and cell-cycle control.

A human multi-pass membrane transporter that assembles an EmrE-like transmembrane core to move thiamine or its precursors across the lipid bilayer. By forming oligomeric complexes and engaging membrane scaffolds, it supports thiamine uptake and intracellular cofactor balance at the cell surface. Its architecture and assembly behavior indicate a proton-coupled alternating-access mechanism that sustains thiamine-dependent metabolism at the plasma membrane.

A cytoplasmic RNA-modifying enzyme that installs pseudouridines in structured RNAs, including mRNA, by catalyzing uridine-to-pseudouridine isomerization through a conserved active center within a RluA-like fold. Its catalytic architecture supports broad RNA recognition and transient assembly with cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein complexes, thereby stabilizing RNA structure and tuning translational efficiency and RNA surveillance pathways.

A soluble phage-encoded transcriptional corepressor that concentrates within a host intracellular nucleoprotein compartment and enforces repression of the viral transcriptional program. It achieves this by assembling multiprotein complexes rather than binding DNA directly, thereby dampening promoter activity without interfering with viral DNA replication. By stabilizing repressive assemblies and constraining RNA polymerase engagement, it helps set the timing of the phage gene-expression cascade.

A multi-pass membrane transporter in rat that uses an alternating-access mechanism to move thyroid hormones across the cell surface. Its major facilitator architecture supports secondary-active transport, enabling low-affinity, high-capacity exchange of T3 and T4 that shapes hormone availability and signaling. By controlling hormone flux at the plasma membrane of polarized cells, it modulates downstream pathways of thyroid hormone utilization and turnover.

An extracellular α-amylase–family enzyme in Klebsiella that uses a GH13 catalytic barrel and a SusG-like C-terminal platform to catalyze sucrose disproportionation, generating glucose and fructose outside the cell. By leveraging a retaining glycosidase scaffold configured for rearrangement chemistry, it initiates disaccharide breakdown and channels products toward uptake systems at the cell surface, coordinating with periplasmic and transporter modules to drive extracellular sucrose utilization.

A secreted human enzyme that accelerates the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide, rapidly buffering proton and bicarbonate levels to stabilize acid–base balance. By shaping extracellular and pericellular pH microdomains, it supports neuronal homeostasis and enhances inhibitory signaling pathways. Its zinc-dependent catalytic core drives fast carbonate interconversion, indirectly tuning anion transport and synaptic transmission in environments where precise pH control is essential.

A multi-pass membrane transporter that uses a major facilitator fold to shuttle neutral and aromatic amino acids across the cell surface. It mediates uptake and exchange of branched-chain amino acids and related substrates, thereby supporting cellular amino acid balance by coupling proton-driven conformational changes to substrate translocation at the plasma membrane. Its broad specificity encompasses hydrophobic/aromatic residues and neutral amino acids, positioning it as a key conduit for isoleucine, valine, and other essential amino acids in human cells.

A nuclear transcriptional repressor that uses an N-terminal repression module to recruit corepressor assemblies and a large array of C2H2 zinc fingers to specify genomic targets. By coupling sequence-directed targeting with assembly of chromatin-silencing machinery, it downregulates gene expression through formation of repressive complexes that compact chromatin and suppress transcription.

A membrane-associated RING E3 ubiquitin ligase in mouse that operates on the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum to catalyze ubiquitin transfer onto target proteins. It modifies ribosomal protein RPS2A and the transcriptional coactivator EP300, thereby coupling ribosome-associated quality control with transcriptional regulation. The RING domain recruits ubiquitin-charged E2 enzymes and promotes isopeptide bond formation on substrate lysines, enabling both degradative and non-degradative ubiquitination that tunes protein turnover and signaling at ER-proximal and nucleocytoplasmic sites.

A single-pass cell-surface adhesion receptor that forms a heterodimeric integrin complex to mediate high-affinity attachment to extracellular matrix and stabilize cell-cell contacts. Its extracellular head and stalk bind matrix ligands and transmit conformational signals that regulate affinity and clustering, while the cytoplasmic tail recruits adaptor proteins to couple adhesion to actin assembly and focal adhesion machinery. Through this bidirectional signaling, it coordinates migration, stress fiber formation, epithelial adhesion, and developmental programs, operating at the plasma membrane within integrin assemblies and integrating with growth factor pathways.

A soluble nuclear serine/threonine kinase that requires cyclin-like regulation to phosphorylate nuclear substrates, including repeats within the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II and checkpoint-associated factors. By tuning transcriptional machinery and checkpoint pathways, it orchestrates gene-expression programs that feed into autophagy and antiviral responses. Its activity is driven by a canonical bilobal kinase core with defined ATP-binding and catalytic motifs, and its nuclear residence positions it to coordinate transcriptional control with stress-adaptive signaling.

A soluble FAD-dependent dehydrogenase in Bacillus subtilis that oxidizes L-proline to Δ1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate, initiating the proline catabolic route toward glutamate. Its redox core transfers electrons from the proline substrate to quinone-like acceptors, coupling amino acid breakdown to cellular energy metabolism. The enzyme operates primarily in the cytoplasm but likely approaches membrane-proximal redox hubs that reoxidize its flavin via quinone pools, thereby integrating proline utilization with broader respiratory pathways.

A small cytoplasmic assembly subunit of the bacterial transcription machinery that organizes and stabilizes the RNA polymerase core. By forming a conserved scaffold that binds other polymerase components, it promotes proper assembly and conformational stability of the enzyme that synthesizes RNA from DNA templates. Through this assembly role it indirectly shapes promoter engagement and elongation, enabling conditions that can attenuate transcription output in the thermophilic cytoplasm.

A large nuclear methyltransferase that uses a SAM-dependent catalytic core to deposit methyl groups onto lysine 79 of histone H3 within assembled nucleosomes. By forming higher-order nuclear assemblies, it recognizes chromatin substrates and catalyzes lysine methylation that modulates transcriptional and DNA repair pathways. Its extended auxiliary regions promote complex formation and nucleosome engagement, enabling efficient histone modification inside the nucleus.

A membrane-embedded acyltransferase that installs palmitate onto diverse cytosolic and membrane-proximal proteins to control their membrane association and signaling competence. By forming a thioester intermediate with palmitoyl-CoA and transferring the acyl group to substrate cysteines, it stabilizes targets at the plasma membrane and within endocytic and phagocytic pathways. This lipidation promotes surface accumulation of cargo in dendrites, tunes innate immune signalosome assembly, and modulates trafficking hubs by palmitoylating small GTPases and key kinases and adaptors.

A nuclear lysine methyltransferase that uses a SET catalytic core supported by N-terminal interaction modules to methylate lysine residues on histone H3 and selected non-histone proteins. By installing monomethyl marks associated with transcription-coupled chromatin states, it assembles and stabilizes nuclear complexes that fine-tune gene expression, often biasing networks toward repression. Its soluble, nucleoplasmic architecture enables broad substrate recognition, including cell-cycle and replication factors, thereby coupling chromatin modification to transcriptional control.

A human multi-pass membrane protein that assembles a transporter-like helical bundle to act as a membrane-associated scaffold for endosomal trafficking. It cycles between cytosolic and membrane-associated pools and concentrates on endosomal and lysosomal membranes, where it likely oligomerizes and recruits sorting machinery to direct cargo toward degradation. By biasing receptor and transporter routing within the endomembrane system, it dampens signaling throughput and thereby attenuates downstream pathways that depend on membrane trafficking dynamics.

A cytoplasmic BTB/POZ-domain scaffold that self-associates to build higher-order assemblies and act as an adaptor for ubiquitin-ligase machinery. By forming multivalent cytosolic complexes, it organizes and dampens delayed rectifier potassium channel output, likely by concentrating channel-associated regulators and ubiquitin-coupled factors that reduce current amplitude or channel abundance.

A cytoplasmic antitoxin that forms a homodimeric DNA-binding scaffold to repress transcription of its operon and cognate toxin within a type II toxin–antitoxin module. By assembling on operator DNA and recruiting transcriptional machinery, it downregulates target genes and, through direct complex formation with the endogenous toxin, neutralizes its activity. This dual sequestration and transcriptional control stabilizes growth under non-stress conditions and modulates stress responses via nucleoid-associated regulatory assemblies.

A soluble mitochondrial non-heme iron oxygenase that uses a TauD-like catalytic core to hydroxylate trimethyllysine, generating gamma-butyrobetaine as the committed intermediate of the carnitine biosynthetic route. By coupling oxygen activation to 2-oxoglutarate-dependent chemistry, it supplies the precursor required for downstream steps that sustain acyl transport and energy metabolism within mitochondria. Its architecture and chemistry indicate a matrix-facing enzyme that assembles transiently with mitochondrial metabolic machinery to channel intermediates efficiently.

A soluble mitochondrial oxygenase that uses alpha-ketoglutarate and molecular oxygen to hydroxylate trimethyllysine, generating gamma-butyrobetaine as a committed step toward carnitine biosynthesis. By coupling non-heme iron chemistry to small-molecule oxidation within the mitochondrial matrix, it feeds the carnitine pathway that supports acyl-group transfer and broader energy metabolism. Its N-terminal scaffold and TauD-like catalytic core cooperate to bind iron and alpha-ketoglutarate, producing succinate and CO2 while channeling intermediates to downstream steps of the pathway.

A nuclear scaffold that integrates a WD-repeat β-propeller with a C-terminal acetyl-lysine–reading module to assemble and stabilize transcriptional and chromatin-remodeling complexes. By docking onto acetylated chromatin and concentrating coactivators and mediator assemblies, it enhances transcriptional output at active loci within the nucleus, acting through multivalent protein binding and chromatin targeting.

A nucleocytoplasmic deubiquitinating enzyme that uses an N-terminal adaptor module to recruit pathway-specific partners and a papain-like catalytic core to hydrolyze ubiquitin from diverse substrates. By reversing ubiquitin tagging, it stabilizes or destabilizes client proteins, edits histone ubiquitination, and tunes the circadian system by preserving the steady-state levels of key clock components. Its soluble architecture supports assembly of higher-order complexes in both cytoplasm and nucleus, where it coordinates substrate capture and catalysis to balance proteostasis and chromatin regulation.

A soluble cytoplasmic metallo–aminopeptidase that assembles into homomultimers and trims N-terminal residues from intracellular peptides to sustain proteostasis and amino acid recycling. Its oligomeric scaffold drives self-association and positions substrates for efficient peptide bond hydrolysis, thereby supporting developmental programs such as mesoderm formation. The enzyme operates in the cytoplasm and functionally couples to pathways adjacent to membrane-bounded organelles where peptide turnover and amino acid supply are integrated.

A cytoplasmic metallo-exopeptidase that assembles into a homo-oligomeric cage and removes N-terminal residues from intracellular peptides. By shaping the cytosolic peptide pool, it supports proteostasis and signaling pathways that influence mesodermal development. Its soluble architecture and oligomerization drive activity in the cytoplasm and in proximity to membrane-bounded organelles where peptide flux and translational pathways converge.

A multi-pass membrane pseudoenzyme that organizes intramembrane assemblies to regulate signaling and secretion. It uses an inactive rhomboid scaffold to bind and modulate membrane-associated proteases and trafficking machinery, thereby restraining intracellular membrane trafficking and secretion. Through this regulatory hub it influences cell proliferation and migration and fine-tunes growth factor receptor pathways, acting at organelle membranes where it assembles and stabilizes complexes rather than catalyzing proteolysis.

A single-pass, ER-anchored RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase that uses a cytosolic zinc-finger catalytic module to recruit E2 conjugating enzymes and assemble ubiquitin on membrane-proximal substrates. By catalyzing ubiquitin transfer at the endoplasmic reticulum, it modulates protein turnover and trafficking within the secretory pathway, thereby shaping signaling and stress-adaptation circuits through targeted ubiquitination.

A soluble cytosolic dipeptidase that assembles as a homodimeric metallo-hydrolase to cleave a broad spectrum of dipeptides and related peptide products, thereby feeding amino acid recycling in the cytoplasm. Its metal-activated active site and dimerization module confer nonspecific hydrolytic activity that supports general peptide turnover and metabolic homeostasis in human cells.

A cell-surface, seven-pass chemosensory receptor in human sensory neurons that transduces extracellular bioactive cues into intracellular second-messenger signals. By activating heterotrimeric G proteins at the plasma membrane, it modulates excitability and transmitter release in nociceptors, thereby influencing pain perception and broader sensory responses. Its mechanism relies on a rhodopsin-like transmembrane core that binds ligands within the helical bundle and couples to canonical G protein pathways to regulate neuronal signaling.

A cytoplasmic RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase that assembles higher-order TRIM complexes to transfer ubiquitin onto selected substrates. Its N-terminal catalytic module works with a coiled-coil scaffold to position the active site, while a C-terminal PRY/SPRY recognition domain confers substrate specificity. Through targeted ubiquitination, it modulates pathways governing apoptosis and differentiation by coupling ubiquitin signaling to transcriptional and cytosolic regulators.

A human cytosolic actin-assembly factor that uses an N-terminal regulatory scaffold to bind Rho-pathway modulators and relieve autoinhibition of a C-terminal actin-assembly engine. By coupling Rho-family signaling to filament nucleation and elongation at membrane-proximal sites, it organizes the cortical actin network and drives cell-shape remodeling. Its soluble pool is recruited to the plasma membrane and phagocytic vesicles where it coordinates morphogenesis through tightly regulated actin dynamics.

A Golgi-resident, single-pass type II membrane enzyme that transfers sulfate from a nucleotide-linked donor onto heparan sulfate chains during proteoglycan maturation. Anchored in the Golgi membrane with a lumenal catalytic domain, it installs 2-hydroxyl sulfate groups on glucosamine residues of heparan sulfate, thereby shaping the sulfation patterns that govern extracellular matrix assembly and growth factor binding. Its membrane-proximal architecture positions the catalytic core to act on nascent glycosaminoglycans within the secretory pathway.

A large cytoplasmic scaffold that uses an N-terminal leucine‑rich repeat array and a C‑terminal PDZ module to organize membrane‑proximal signaling assemblies. By capturing the cytoplasmic tails of membrane receptors and assembling adaptor complexes, it regulates neurotransmitter receptor abundance at postsynaptic sites and directs protein targeting to defined membrane territories. The same membrane‑tethered assemblies attenuate cytosolic innate immune pathways, dampening NOD‑dependent signaling and downstream chemokine outputs. It functions as a soluble organizer at the inner face of the plasma membrane and within the cytoplasm.

An inner-membrane–anchored, ATP-dependent zinc metalloprotease in human mitochondria that couples a powerful AAA+ unfoldase to a proteolytic chamber to process and degrade mitochondrial proteins. By mechanically extracting and unfolding substrates and then cleaving them within its catalytic core, it maintains mitochondrial proteostasis, supports maturation and turnover of imported and assembly intermediates, and thereby contributes to the regulation of mitochondrial morphology and function.

A soluble Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent hydroxylase in Neurospora crassa that installs a hydroxyl group during oxygenation reactions. It uses an internal iron–2-oxoglutarate catalytic core to hydroxylate gamma-butyrobetaine with high efficiency, producing L-carnitine, and also accepts taurine as a substrate. By coupling oxygen activation to 2-oxoglutarate decarboxylation, it drives a key step in mitochondrial-associated carnitine and betaine metabolism, supporting acyl-group handling and redox-balanced pathways in the mitochondrial compartment.

A cytoplasmic phosphoinositide-cleaving enzyme that assembles a membrane-targeted catalytic core to hydrolyze phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into diacylglycerol and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate. It uses a pleckstrin homology module to dock at PIP2-rich membranes, EF-hand motifs to sense calcium, and a paired catalytic center to execute phosphodiester cleavage, with C2 and extended C-terminal regions stabilizing membrane association and regulatory coupling to heterotrimeric G-protein pathways. Through this mechanism it drives intracellular signaling by converting membrane phosphoinositides into second messengers and sustaining glycerophospholipid and phosphoinositide metabolism.

A soluble scaffold localized to the magnetosome that uses a Tim44-like core to organize protein assemblies controlling biogenesis of the iron-storage compartment.
